text:
LAFAYETTE – On October 29, 2026, United States District Judge David C. Joseph sentenced Henry Nicola Meyer , 26, of Eunice, to 42 months in federal prison for Possession of Ammunition by a Convicted Felon and Possession of Five or More False Identification Documents, followed by three years of supervised release. Meyer previously pled guilty to the charges on July 9, 2026.

According to court documents, on October 9, 2025, the Federal Bureau of Investigation (FBI) and Eunice Police Department (EPD) executed a Louisiana search warrant at Meyer's residence when Meyer was on probation. Agents then located a padlocked bedroom containing Meyer's personal belongings and discovered a partially constructed “ghost gun” (a homemade, unregistered firearm) and 25 rounds of 9mm ammunition. Meyer admitted possessing the ammunition and acknowledged he was a convicted felon prohibited from doing so. Agents also recovered eight high-quality fake driver’s licenses bearing Meyer’s photograph, including licenses represented to be from Kentucky, Alaska, Colorado, and Georgia. Meyer admitted he knew the licenses were fraudulent and intended to use them unlawfully to misrepresent his identity.

U.S. Attorney Zachary A. Keller for the Western District of Louisiana made the announcement.

FBI and EPD investigated this case. It was prosecuted by United States Attorney Zachary A. Keller with the assistance of Paralegal Specialist Joanne Henry-Mills.

This case was prosecuted as part of Project Safe Neighborhoods (PSN), the Department of Justice’s nationwide initiative that brings federal, state, local, and tribal law enforcement, prosecutors, and other public safety partners together to coordinate efforts to combat violent crime and make communities safe. Coordinated by U.S. Attorneys’ offices in each of the 94 federal districts, PSN is tailored to particular communities to strategically address specific violent crime and public safety challenges. As a key component of Operation Take Back America, PSN serves a central role in the Department’s commitment to make our country safe. PSN emphasizes three core principles: rapid federal response to violent crime and criminal offenders; strong, strategic partnerships among law enforcement at all levels; and accountability and deterrence through the prosecution of the most serious, readily provable offenses and other strategies. These efforts complement and strengthen President Trump’s Homeland Security Task Forces, ensuring a comprehensive federal response to the most pressing public safety issues facing communities. Learn more at www.justice.gov/psn.

You may find a copy of this press release (and any updates) on the website of the United States Attorney’s Office for the Western District of Louisiana at www.justice.gov/usao-wdla.

Related court documents and information may be found on the website of the District Court for the Western District of Louisiana at www.lawd.uscourts.gov or at https://www.lawd.uscourts.gov/cmecf-pacer, under Case Number 6:26-CR-00136.

BOSTON – A member of the Boston Chapter of the Trinitarios pleaded guilty on Oct. 28, 2026 to racketeering drug charges, including a home invasion robbery in July 2025 in Lawrence, Mass.

Yoldari Tejeda Coronado, a/k/a “Nonoy,” 25, of Lawrence, pleaded guilty to conspiracy to conduct enterprise affairs through a pattern of racketeering activity (also known as “racketeering conspiracy” or “RICO conspiracy”). U.S. Senior District Court Judge Nathaniel M. Gorton scheduled sentencing for Jan. 27, 2027. Coronado was arrested and charged in December 2025 as part of a related case.

The Trinitarios is a violent criminal enterprise comprised of thousands of members across the United States. The Trinitarios adhere to a Magna Carta, employ an internal hierarchy to coordinate and execute violence, and undertake extensive efforts to maintain the secrecy of the organization and its members.

During the plea hearing, Coronado admitted that he was a member of the Boston Chapter of the Trinitarios. Cooperating witnesses, social media images and tattoos confirmed that he was a member since at least 2023. Coronado admitted that he conspired to commit a home invasion in Lawrence in July 2025. During the home invasion, two gunmen forced an individual into their residence and robbed the residence. Further investigation revealed that a vehicle associated with Coronado’s girlfriend was identified as being used by the robbers.

Coronado was also captured on recording, offering to conduct the robbery of a drug stash house. During that recording, Coronado discussed planning the robbery with undercover agents posing as individuals responsible for transporting a large quantity of cocaine for a Mexican drug cartel. Coronado discussed details of the planned robbery and the other individuals who would be involved and agreed to take multiple kilograms of cocaine as payment.

Additionally, Coronado was the subject of a recorded conversation involving the State Supreme, Enmanuel Paula-Cabral, a/k/a “Nelfew,” who described Coronado as having conducted a robbery of a drug dealer. Paula-Cabral discussed being contacted by the drug dealer and that he used his authority as leader of the Trinitarios to have Coronado, a subordinate member in the gang, return the drugs to the drug dealer.

In February 2025 , federal racketeering charges were unsealed against 22 leaders and members of the Trinitarios. The charges were the result of a multijurisdictional investigation, which began in the aftermath of four murders as well as a series of attempted murders and shootings that took place in Lynn in 2023, allegedly committed by the Trinitarios criminal enterprise and its members. On June 9, 2026 , additional federal racketeering and drug charges were unsealed charging 26 additional leaders, members and associates of the Lawrence, Haverhill and Boston Chapters of the gang. According to court documents, the Trinitarios have allegedly participated in five additional murders in Essex County since 2017, bringing the total of federally charged murders to 11, and the total number of federally charged defendants to 56.

The charge of conspiracy to conduct enterprise affairs through a pattern of racketeering activity provides for a sentence of up to life in prison, five years of supervised release and a fine of up to $250,000. Sentences are imposed by a federal district court judge based upon the U.S. Sentencing Guidelines and statutes which govern the determination of a sentence in a criminal case.

United States Attorney Leah B. Foley; Jeff Grimming, Acting Special Agent in Charge of Homeland Security Investigations in New England; Ted E. Docks, Special Agent in Charge, Federal Bureau of Investigation, Boston Division; Essex County District Attorney Paul F. Tucker; Massachusetts State Police Colonel Geoffrey D. Noble; and Lynn Police Chief Christopher P. Reddy made the announcement today. Valuable assistance was provided by the Manchester, N.H. Police Department. Assistant U.S. Attorney Philip A. Mallard of the Organized Crime & Gang Unit is prosecuting the case.

This case is part of the Homeland Security Task Force (HSTF) initiative established by Executive Order 14159, Protecting the American People Against Invasion. The HSTF is a whole-of-government partnership dedicated to eliminating criminal cartels, foreign gangs, transnational criminal organizations, and human smuggling and trafficking rings operating in the United States and abroad. Through historic interagency collaboration, the HSTF directs the full might of United States law enforcement towards identifying, investigating, and prosecuting the full spectrum of crimes committed by these organizations, which have long fueled violence and instability within our borders. In performing this work, the HSTF places special emphasis on investigating and prosecuting those engaged in child trafficking or other crimes involving children. The HSTF further utilizes all available tools to prosecute and remove the most violent criminal aliens from the United States. HSTF Boston is comprised of agents and officers from HSI, FBI, DEA, ATF, USMS, IRS-CI, USPIS, DOL-OIG, DSS and CBP as well as several state and local law enforcement agencies, with the prosecution being led by the United States Attorney’s Office for the District of Massachusetts.

BOSTON – A Dominican man unlawfully residing in Salem, Mass. was charged by criminal complaint allegedly unlawfully obtaining approximately $16,000 in MassHealth benefits and aggravated identity theft.

Cledis German Romero, 40, has been charged with healthcare benefit fraud and aggravated identity theft and appeared in federal court in Boston on Nov. 3, 2026. He has been detained pending further proceedings.

According to the charging documents, German Romero allegedly used the stolen identity of a U.S. citizen to obtain Massachusetts state driver’s licenses and healthcare benefits, including approximately $16,205 in MassHealth benefits. German Romero also allegedly used the stolen identity of the U.S. citizen in connection with multiple arrests and criminal convictions in Massachusetts, including resisting arrest and conspiracy to violate the controlled substances act.

The charge of making false statements relating to a health care program provides for a sentence of up to five years in prison, three years of supervised release and a fine of $250,000. The charge of aggravated identity theft provides for a mandatory consecutive sentence of two years and one year of supervised release. The defendant is subject to deportation upon completion of any sentence imposed. Sentences are imposed by a federal district court judge based upon the U.S. Sentencing Guidelines and statutes which govern the determination of a sentence in a criminal case.

United States Attorney Leah B. Foley and Jeff Grimming, Acting Special Agent in Charge of Homeland Security Investigations in New England made the announcement today. Assistant U.S. Attorney Catherine Conroy of the Major Crimes Unit is prosecuting the case.

On March 26, 2026 , United States Attorney Leah B. Foley announced the creation of the Benefit & Voter Fraud Team, a district-wide initiative established in response to the rampant fraud being uncovered across Massachusetts. Members of the public are encouraged to report suspected benefit fraud in Massachusetts by calling 1-855-SCAM-MA-1 (855-722-6621).

On April 7, 2026, the Department of Justice announced the creation of the National Fraud Enforcement Division . The Fraud Division is investigating and prosecuting those who commit fraud against the American people. The Department’s work to combat fraud supports President Trump’s Task Force to Eliminate Fraud, a whole-of-government effort chaired by Vice President J.D. Vance to eliminate fraud, waste, and abuse within Federal benefit programs.

The details contained in the charging document are allegations. The defendant is presumed to be innocent unless and until proven guilty beyond a reasonable doubt in the court of law.

RAPID CITY - United States Attorney Ron Parsons announced today that U.S. District Judge Karen E. Schreier has sentenced a Lead, South Dakota, woman convicted of Assault Resulting in Serious Bodily Injury. The sentencing took place on October 30, 2026.

Vivian Rose One Feather, age 32, was sentenced to three years and five months in federal prison, followed by three years of supervised release, and ordered to pay a $100 special assessment to the Federal Crime Victims Fund.

One Feather was indicted by a federal grand jury in May 2026. She pleaded guilty on August 7, 2026.

On Valentine’s Day 2026, One Feather and her boyfriend saw a man walking alongside the road near Little Eagle, South Dakota. One Feather believed the man had wronged her boyfriend’s mother. One Feather and her boyfriend exited their vehicle and began assaulting the male. While the boyfriend used only his fists, One Feather struck the man with a metal bar and kicked him, even after he fell to the ground. One Feather only stopped when her boyfriend pulled her away. The male lost consciousness during the assault and experienced extreme pain. He required sutures and staples for several injuries to his head and experienced dizziness for months after the assault.

This matter was prosecuted by the U.S. Attorney’s Office because the Major Crimes Act, a federal statute, mandates that certain violent crimes alleged to have occurred in Indian country be prosecuted in Federal Court as opposed to State Court.

This case was investigated by the Bureau of Indian Affairs – Office of Justice Services. Assistant U.S. Attorney Carl Thunem prosecuted the case.

One Feather was remanded to the custody of the U.S. Marshals Service to serve her federal sentence.

HARRISBURG - The United States Attorney’s Office for the Middle District of Pennsylvania announced that Takquasha Beatty, age 31, of York, Pennsylvania, was sentenced on October 15, 2026, to four years in prison by United States District Judge Keli M. Neary for trafficking cocaine.

According to United States Attorney Brian D. Miller, a grand jury indicted Takquasha Beatty and others for their role in a conspiracy to traffic cocaine in York, Pennsylvania with kilograms of cocaine smuggled in from Puerto Rico into York. On March 15, 2023, law enforcement searched Beatty’s home in York where they found cocaine hidden in a children’s toy, a cash counting machine in the kitchen, $35,700 in cash, a digital scale for weighing drugs, a loaded gun, and other materials indicative of drug trafficking. Other locations linked to the drug trafficking conspiracy were searched the same day and similar evidence was recovered. Two weeks later, law enforcement intercepted 30 kilograms of cocaine shipped from Puerto Rico to York, destined for this same drug trafficking group.

At sentencing, Judge Neary emphasized the seriousness of the crime and the scope of the drug trafficking conspiracy. When imposing sentence, Judge Neary also emphasized that Beatty allowed this drug trafficking to happen in her home where her four small children lived. In March 2026, Beatty pled guilty to conspiracy to trafficking cocaine.

The following co-defendants in this case also pled guilty to conspiracy to traffic cocaine:

Juan Escalera-Carrasquillo, age 27, York, PA – pending sentencing;

Daniel Velez-Olivero, age 39, York, PA – sentenced to 120 months in prison, 5 years of supervised release, $200 fine, and $100 special assessment;

Gerald J. Calcano, age 33, York, PA – sentenced to 120 months in prison, 5 years of supervised release, $100 special assessment;

Kevin Marrero-Morales, age 31, York PA – sentenced to 120 months in prison, 5 years of supervised release, $500 fine and $100 special assessment; and

Jorge Angel Rivera-Ortiz, age 26. York, PA – sentenced to time served, three years of supervised release, $100 special assessment.

Co-defendant Reynaldo Vargas Seda pled guilty to possession of a short-barreled rifle in furtherance of drug trafficking. He is scheduled for sentencing on February 9, 2027.

Press Statement

Marco Rubio, Secretary of State

November 3, 2026

On behalf of the United States of America, I congratulate the people of Panama on the 123rd anniversary of your independence. Panama is one of our most important partners, and we will continue to stand with you as you recover from the recent earthquake. Our strong partnership allowed us to deliver humanitarian, logistical, and technical assistance within 24 hours of the disaster.

We marked significant advances in our relationship this year. Panama joined the Shield of the Americas, Americas Counter Cartel Coalition, and Pax Silica. Together, we showed our commitment to the Panama Canal’s security during PANAMAX, the first large-scale live exercise in 14 years. In the year ahead, we will deepen our security partnership and pursue new trade and investment opportunities. Panama is making historic investments in the Canal and seeking investment in technology, cybersecurity, and other critical infrastructure, as well as health and education. I wish the people of Panama a joyous celebration.

By Staff Sgt. Kenyel Jones
4th Psychological Operations Group Public Affairs
FORT BRAGG, N.C. — Soldiers assigned to the 4th Psychological Operations Group are developing practical cooking and nutrition skills through a meal preparation program that complements the unit's newly renovated barracks kitchen.
The kitchen, which officially opened in September 2026, provides Soldiers with a functional space to prepare meals while supporting the group's efforts to improve barracks living conditions and promote healthier food choices.
Jessie Anderson, a performance dietitian supporting psychological operations Soldiers, said the renovation addressed a need for improved cooking facilities for Soldiers living in the barracks.
According to Anderson, the barracks are located far from the dining facility, and although Soldiers receive basic allowance for subsistence, they previously lacked a functional kitchen to prepare their own meals.
Anderson worked alongside unit leadership to help develop the kitchen's layout and design, creating a space where Soldiers could cook independently and participate in hands-on nutrition education.
The renovated facility also allows Anderson to move beyond office-based instruction and provide practical demonstrations of food preparation, cooking techniques and nutrition label reading.
Through the commissary tour and meal preparation class, Anderson teaches Soldiers how to make nutritious food choices, manage grocery expenses and develop sustainable eating habits.
"You have to enjoy it to sustain it," Anderson said.
The class begins at the Fort Bragg South Post Commissary, where Soldiers learn to compare food options, shop within a budget and select ingredients before returning to the renovated barracks kitchen for hands-on meal preparation.
Anderson's meal preparation roadmap outlines a goal of producing 20 meal and snack containers, including six breakfasts, 10 lunch and dinner portions and four snack containers, at an estimated grocery cost of $68 to $80.
Recipes include chia pudding overnight oats, sweet potato taco bowls, burritos and chocolate peanut butter energy bites.
For Pfc. Daniel Cedeño, assigned to Headquarters and Headquarters Company, 4th Psychological Operations Group, the class provided an opportunity to develop cooking and nutrition skills he had rarely practiced before.
When asked how often he prepared his own meals before participating, Cedeño said, "Probably never."
Cedeño said the experience helped him become more aware of ingredients in food products and how some products may be marketed as healthy despite their nutritional content. He also appreciated his unit's investment in providing the renovated kitchen and nutrition program.
"It means that they care," Cedeño said. "That they support their Soldiers."
Anderson currently offers the class twice a month and hopes to expand the program as more Soldiers become aware of the opportunity. Future classes could focus on preparing individual meals while teaching Soldiers about nutrition, ingredients and cooking techniques.
Anderson emphasized that the program is designed to make preparing nutritious meals practical and manageable, helping Soldiers build confidence in the kitchen while reducing food waste and the cost of dining out.
A Soldier, assigned to Alpha Company, 9th Psychological Operations Battalion, said the renovated kitchen exceeded his expectations. Although Barnes does not reside in the barracks, he recognized the value of providing Soldiers with a functional space to prepare their own meals.
"The kitchen is very nice," Barnes said. "Six stovetops are great. I love the deep-dish sinks as well."
By combining improved barracks facilities with practical nutrition education, the 4th Psychological Operations Group (Airborne) is providing Soldiers with opportunities to develop independent cooking skills, manage food expenses and make informed decisions about their daily nutrition.
title: Fort Bragg Soldiers Build Nutrition Skills Through Renovated Barracks Kitchen, Meal Prep Program

Tallahassee, Florida – Frederick Allen Smith, Jr., 54, of Madison, Florida, pleaded guilty in federal court to possession with intent to distribute 50 grams or more of methamphetamine and 500 grams or more of a mixture containing methamphetamine, possession of a firearm in furtherance of a drug trafficking offense, and possession of a firearm by a convicted felon. The plea was announced by John P. Heekin, United States Attorney for the Northern District of Florida.

U.S. Attorney Heekin said: “Our state and federal law enforcement partners are cleaning up our streets and removing dangerous armed drug traffickers from our communities, and my office is backing up those efforts with aggressive prosecutions to ensure anyone who peddles deadly drugs in the Northern District of Florida is kept behind federal bars for as long as possible. Under the leadership of President Donald J. Trump and Attorney General Todd Blanche, we are devoting the full might of the Department of Justice toward delivering the safe, drug-free streets that our citizens deserve.”

Court documents reflect that in May 2026, law enforcement executed a search warrant at the defendant’s residence, where deputies seized 703 grams of methamphetamine, a loaded handgun, ammunition, and more than $17,000 in cash. The defendant has multiple prior felony convictions dating back to 2005 and was legally prohibited from possessing firearms or ammunition.

The defendant faces a minimum of 10 years’ imprisonment and up to life imprisonment on the possession with intent to distribute methamphetamine count; a minimum of 5 years’ imprisonment consecutive to other sentences on the possession of a firearm in furtherance count; and up to 15 years’ imprisonment on the possession of a firearm by a convicted felon count.

The case involved a joint investigation by the Drug Enforcement Administration, the Bureau of Alcohol, Tobacco, Firearms and Explosives, and the Madison County Sheriff’s Office. Assistant United States Attorney Emma Schwan is prosecuting the case.

Sentencing is scheduled for November 9, 2026, at 1:00pm at the United States Courthouse in Tallahassee before United States District Judge Robert L. Hinkle.

SIOUX FALLS - United States Attorney Ron Parsons announced today that U.S. District Judge Karen E. Schreier has sentenced a Sioux Falls man convicted of possession of a firearm by a prohibited person. The sentencing took place on November 2, 2026.

Dakota Thorstenson, 30, was sentenced to 2 years and 6 months in federal prison, followed by three years of supervised release, and ordered to pay a $100 special assessment to the Federal Crime Victims Fund.

Thorstenson was indicted for possession of a firearm by a prohibited person by a federal grand jury in May 2026. He pleaded guilty on August 11, 2026.

In April of this year, Thorstenson was the driver of a vehicle involved in two automobile accidents in rapid succession in southern Sioux Falls. As a result of his involvement in the two accidents, Thorstenson was taken into custody by local law enforcement. He was searched and a pistol was found on him. Thorstenson is prohibited from possessing firearms due to felony convictions for Distribution or Possession with Intent to Distribute Marijuana from 2015 in Brookings County, Simple Assault on a Law Enforcement Officer from 2015 in Brookings County, and Simple Assault, Third or Subsequent Offense from 2022 in Minnehaha County.

This case was investigated by the Bureau of Alcohol, Tobacco, Firearms, and Explosives. Special Assistant U.S. Attorney Ryan McFall prosecuted the case.

Thorstenson was immediately remanded to the custody of the U.S. Marshals Service.
title: Sioux Falls Man Sentenced to 2 years in Federal Prison for Possession of a Firearm by a Prohibited Person

BOSTON – A Holliston, Mass. man pleaded guilty on Oct. 27, 2026 in federal court in Boston to sexually exploiting a minor.

Wilson Fabian Mizhirumbay Granda, 23, pleaded guilty to one count of sexual exploitation of children. U.S. District Court Judge Allison D. Burroughs scheduled sentencing for Jan. 20, 2027. Granda was charged in September 2026 and is currently in Massachusetts state custody on an unrelated criminal case.

Between August and September 2023, Granda coerced a minor victim to travel to Massachusetts and engage in sexually explicit conduct. Granda met the minor victim on a social media site, knew she was underage and lied about his own age. Granada later recorded himself having sex with minor victim on a number of occasions.

Granda has prior state convictions in Hampshire Country Superior Court for rape of a child and enticing a child under 16, for which he was sentenced in May 2024 to four years and one day in state prison to be followed by five years of probation. Currently, Granda also has pending charges in Norfolk County for rape of child with force, rape of child and enticing a child under 16 related to another minor.

The charge of sexual exploitation of children provides for a sentence of up to 30 years in prison, a lifetime of supervised release and a fine of up to $250,000. Sentences are imposed by a federal district court judge based upon the U.S. Sentencing Guidelines and statutes which govern the determination of a sentence in a criminal case.

United States Attorney Leah B. Foley and Ted E. Docks, Special Agent in Charge of the Federal Bureau of Investigation, Boston Division made the announcement today. Valuable assistance was provided by the Holliston, Scituate (R.I.), Amherst, Westminster, Medway, Worcester, Millis and UMass Lowell Police Departments; and the Middlesex County, Hampshire County, Northwestern County, Norfolk County and Worcester County District Attorney’s Offices. The case is being prosecuted by Assistant U.S. Attorneys David G. Tobin and Jessica L. Soto of the Criminal Division. This case was brought as part of Project Safe Childhood, a nationwide initiative to combat the growing epidemic of child sexual exploitation and abuse, launched in May 2006 by the Department of Justice. Led by the U.S. Attorneys’ Offices and the DOJ’s Child Exploitation and Obscenity Section, Project Safe Childhood marshals federal, state, and local resources to locate, apprehend, and prosecute individuals who exploit children, as well as identify and rescue victims. For more information about Project Safe Childhood, please visit https://www.justice.gov/psc .

SAVANNAH, Georgia: Several defendants pleaded guilty in district court for charges including distribution of methamphetamine, fentanyl possession, and possession of a firearm by a convicted felon.

The sentences were imposed in U.S. District Court and announced by Margaret E. “Meg” Heap, U.S. Attorney for the Southern District of Georgia.

Jason Chapman , a/k/a “Shane Copeland”, 50, of Waynesville, was sentenced to 102 months in prison followed by three years of supervised release after pleading guilty to Distribution of More than 5 Grams of Methamphetamine.

According to court documents and testimony, in February 2025, investigators with the Drug Enforcement Administration began an investigation into drug trafficking activities of the defendant. Special agents with the DEA determined through various means of investigation that Chapman sold quantities of methamphetamine in Brantley County.

Kyle Ashley Edmunds , 44, of Augusta, was sentenced to 96 months in prison and a $2,500 fine followed by three years of supervised release after pleading guilty to Possession with Intent to Distribute Fentanyl.

According to court documents and testimony, in April 2025, Edmunds was the subject of an investigation based on illegal firearms possession despite prior felony convictions when investigators determined that the defendant was actively selling illegal narcotics, including methamphetamine and fentanyl.

Keith L. Polite , 41, of Thomson, was sentenced to 57 months in prison and a $2,000 fine followed by three years of supervised release after pleading guilty to Possession of a Firearm by a Convicted Felon.

According to court documents and testimony, in December 2024, Polite was found in possession of a firearm, a Sterling Arms, Model 300, .25-caliber pistol and a DPMS model A-15, .223-caliber rifle. Under federal law, it is prohibited for previously convicted felons to possess firearms or ammunition.

Hunter Tucker Baxley , 32, of Evans, was sentenced to 46 months in prison and a $10,000 fine followed by three years of supervised release after pleading guilty to Possession of a Firearm by a Convicted Felon.

According to court documents and testimony, in August 2025, Baxley was found in possession of a firearm, a Fabrique Nationale, 509 Tactical, 9 mm pistol during an encounter with the Columbia County Sheriff’s Office. Under federal law, it is prohibited for previously convicted felons to possess firearms or ammunition.

There is no parole in the federal system.

“Our priority is to ensure that individuals that violate the law are removed from the streets of our community,” said U.S. Attorney Heap. “Through effective interagency cooperation with our law enforcement partners, we are ensuring those that violate the law are brought to justice.”

These cases were investigated by the Bureau of Alcohol, Tobacco, Firearms and Explosive, the Drug Enforcement Administration, Brantley County Sheriff’s Office, Columbia County Sheriff’s Office, Richmond County Sheriff’s Office, and additional law enforcement agencies.

These cases were prosecuted for the United States by Southern District of Georgia Assistant U.S. Attorneys Jennifer J. Kirkland, Henry W. Syms Jr., and Kelsey L. Scanlon.
title: Multiple defendants sentenced to federal prison in separate cases

MARTINSBURG, WEST VIRGINIA – A former employee of the Berkeley County Sheriff’s Office has admitted her role in a years‑long fraud and embezzlement scheme that targeted vulnerable individuals and public funds, U.S. Attorney Matthew L. Harvey announced today.

Lisa Lee French, 48, of Martinsburg, admitted that between 2007 and October 2024, she conspired to steal cash payments collected by the Sheriff’s Office and to manipulate conservatorship and estate accounts overseen by the office. French acknowledged issuing fraudulent checks, forging signatures, misusing a sheriff’s signature stamp, and diverting funds for her personal benefit.

“Fraud on this scale harms not only those directly targeted, but the entire Berkeley County community. We are committed to ensuring accountability and protecting the integrity of our public offices,” said U.S. Attorney Matthew L. Harvey.

“Fraud on this scale harms not only those directly targeted, but the entire Berkeley County community. We are committed to ensuring accountability and protecting the integrity of our public offices,” said U.S. Attorney Matthew L. Harvey.

The victims include Berkeley County taxpayers, individuals under conservatorship, and the Berkeley County Sheriff’s Office itself.

According to court documents, the scheme involved more than 700 fraudulent transactions, over 550 of them forged checks, connected to at least 59 conservator bank accounts. In total, the fraud amounted to nearly $3 million.

French has agreed to pay $2,737,932 in restitution to the identified victims.

A second defendant, Barbara Gail Gooden, is awaiting trial on March 23, 2027. Read the original press release here .

Senior Litigation Counsel Andrew Cogar is prosecuting the case. The investigation was conducted by the Federal Bureau of Investigation, the Berkeley County Sheriff’s Office, and the West Virginia State Auditor’s Office.

On April 7, the Department of Justice announced the formation of the National Fraud Enforcement Division (“Fraud Division”), which focuses on investigating and prosecuting fraud against the American public. This effort supports the President’s Task Force to Eliminate Fraud, a whole‑of‑government initiative chaired by the Vice President to address fraud, waste, and abuse in federal benefit programs.

U.S. Magistrate Judge Robert W. Trumble presided.
title: Former Berkeley County Sheriff’s Office Employee Admits Guilt in Multi-Million-Dollar Fraud Scheme

ST. LOUIS – U.S. District Judge Cristian M. Stevens on Tuesday sentenced a convicted felon from St. Louis to 115 months in prison for shooting and wounding a man in March.

Shan Mims, 39, admitted in July that he used a stolen .380 caliber handgun to shoot the man on March 17, 2026. He also admitted that St. Louis Metropolitan Police Department officers found the gun and cocaine base in his bedroom in a court-approved search nine days later.

The shooting was captured on surveillance video at Mims’ apartment complex. The video shows Mims throwing a water bottle at the victim’s car as it drove by. Mims then approached the victim’s car with his hand inside his jacket, as if he had a gun. In response, the victim opened his car door and produced a handgun. Mims pulled his own and they exchanged gunfire. After shooting the victim, Mims ran down a sidewalk and out of view of the video camera as the victim closed his car door. Mims then circled back into view of the video camera and stood behind a tree pointing his firearm at the victim. The victim fired once at Mims before driving off.

At the time, Mims was on supervised release, having pleaded guilty in U.S. District Court to being a felon in possession of a firearm and possession with intent to distribute a controlled substance in a 2022 case. He was sentenced to 46 months in prison for those offenses.

The St. Louis Metropolitan Police Department investigated the case. Assistant U.S. Attorney J. Christian Goeke prosecuted the case.
title: St. Louis Felon Who Shot and Wounded Man Sentenced to 115 Months in Prison

HARRISBURG - The United States Attorney’s Office for the Middle District of Pennsylvania announced that Tyreese Nealy, age 27, of Harrisburg, Pennsylvania, was sentenced on October 22, 2026, to 60 months’ imprisonment by United States District Judge Keli M. Neary for distribution of methamphetamine.

According to United States Attorney Brian D. Miller, Nealy was sentenced for his role in the drug trafficking and firearms trafficking conspiracy that was the subject of an undercover investigation conducted by the U.S. Bureau of Alcohol, Tobacco, Firearms and Explosives in conjunction with the Pennsylvania Office of Attorney General. During the investigation, undercover officers purchased over three kilograms of methamphetamine, 1,600 fentanyl pills and seven firearms from the conspirators. As a part of the investigation of the conspiracy, Nealy sold to an undercover investigator 171 grams of methamphetamine.

At sentencing, Judge Neary noted the seriousness of the crime and impact that drug trafficking has had on the Harrisburg community. The judge also recognized that Nealy lacked a significant criminal history and imposed the mandatory minimum punishment of 60 months.

Co-defendants Devonte Betts, Lamar Waters, and Rodney McMillian entered guilty pleas to drug trafficking offenses. McMillian was sentenced on October 1, 2026, to 188 months in prison. The other two co-defendants are pending sentencing.

The U.S. Bureau of Alcohol, Tobacco, Firearms and Explosives and the Pennsylvania Office of Attorney General investigated the case. Assistant United States Attorney Michael A. Consiglio prosecuted the case.

Alien from Canada Charged with Falsely Claiming to be a US Citizen to Register to Vote
KANSAS CITY, Mo. — An alien from Canada was arrested and charged with falsely claiming to be a U.S. citizen to register to vote. The U.S. Attorney’s Office for the Western District of Missouri made the announcement. U.S. Citizenship and Immigration Services assisted the investigation.
Christopher Doucet, 68, was indicted by a federal grand jury for allegedly falsely claiming U.S. citizenship to register to vote.
Doucet was born in Canada and immigrated to the United States as a child, becoming a lawful permanent resident. Lawful permanent residents are not allowed to vote in federal, state or local elections in Missouri. Doucet, knowing he was not a U.S, citizen, registered to vote in Jackson County, Missouri, on Jan. 30, 2024. On his voter registration card, Doucet answered “Yes” to the question that asked, “Are you a citizen of the United States of America?” He signed his name under the certification that read, “I hereby certify that I am a citizen of the United States.” A warning on the bottom of the voter registration card advises that a conviction for making a false statement may result in a fine or imprisonment. On April 2, 2024, Doucet voted in a general municipal election in Independence, Missouri.
The charges contained in the indictment are simply accusations and are not evidence of guilt. Evidence supporting the charges must be presented to a federal trial jury that will be responsible for determining whether the defendant is guilty or not.
If convicted, Doucet is subject to a sentence of up to five years in prison and a fine of up to $250,000. The maximum statutory sentence is outlined by Congress and is provided here for informational purposes. The court will determine Doucet’s sentence based on the advisory sentencing guidelines and other statutory factors.
This was investigated by Immigration and Customs Enforcement’s Homeland Security Investigations with assistance from USCIS and is being prosecuted by the U.S. Attorney’s Office for the Western District of Missouri.
To report suspected immigration benefit fraud or abuse to USCIS, please use the USCIS Tip Form.
For more information on USCIS and its programs, please visit uscis.gov or follow us on X, Instagram, YouTube, Facebook and LinkedIn.

SACRAMENTO, Calif. — Abner Estrada Cruz, 27, of Honduras, was sentenced Monday by U.S. District Judge Dale A. Drozd to 14 years in prison for conspiracy to distribute and possess with intent to distribute at least 400 grams of fentanyl, U.S. Attorney Eric Grant announced.

According to court documents, Cruz was a leader and organizer of a Honduran drug trafficking organization operating out of Honduras, Oakland, California, and Portland, Oregon. Through at least seven intermediaries, Cruz coordinated the sale of 14 pounds of fentanyl powder into the Eastern District of California. He was ultimately extradited from Honduras to face the charges in this case.

The Drug Enforcement Administration, the Federal Bureau of Investigation, Homeland Security Investigations, and the U.S. Marshals Service conducted the investigation with assistance from the Butte County Sheriff’s Office, the Bureau of Alcohol, Tobacco, Firearms and Explosives, the California Department of Corrections and Rehabilitation, the Sacramento County Sheriff’s Office, the California Highway Patrol, the California Department of Justice Division of Law Enforcement’s Bureau of Investigation, and the Yolo County District Attorney’s Office. Assistant U.S. Attorney Cameron L. Desmond prosecuted the case.

On May 11, 2026, Cruz pleaded guilty. Below is the status of Cruz’s co-defendants in related cases:

On May 18, 2026, Carlos Samir Colindrez-Erazo pleaded guilty to conspiracy to distribute and possess with intent to distribute at least 400 grams of fentanyl. He is scheduled to be sentenced Dec. 14, 2026.

On July 27, 2026, Aronis Jose Hernandez-Aguilar pleaded guilty to distribution of at least 400 grams of fentanyl. He is scheduled to be sentenced on Jan. 25, 2027.

On Sept. 21, 2026, Yahir Alexander Arteaga Cruz pleaded guilty to conspiracy to distribute and possess with intent to distribute at least 400 grams of fentanyl and four counts of distribution of fentanyl. He is scheduled to be sentenced on Jan. 11, 2027.

This case is part of the Homeland Security Task Force (HSTF) initiative established by Executive Order 14159, Protecting the American People Against Invasion. The HSTF is a whole-of-government partnership dedicated to eliminating criminal cartels, foreign gangs, transnational criminal organizations, and human smuggling and trafficking rings operating in the United States and abroad. Through historic interagency collaboration, the HSTF directs the full might of United States law enforcement towards identifying, investigating, and prosecuting the full spectrum of crimes committed by these organizations, which have long fueled violence and instability within our borders. In performing this work, the HSTF places special emphasis on investigating and prosecuting those engaged in child trafficking or other crimes involving children. The HSTF further utilizes all available tools to prosecute and remove the most violent criminal aliens from the United States. HSTF Sacramento is composed of agents and officers from Homeland Security Investigations, the Federal Bureau of Investigation, the Drug Enforcement Administration, Northern California High Intensity Drug Trafficking Area, Central Valley High Intensity Drug Trafficking Area, and the Sacramento County Sheriff’s Office with the prosecution being led by the United States Attorney’s Office for the Eastern District of California.

The Atlanta-based office was the only U.S. Attorney’s Office in the country to receive multiple team awards.

Hertzberg. “Their exceptional talent, unwavering dedication, and commitment to pursuing justice exemplify the highest ideals of public service and help to make our district safer.”

The Director’s Awards recognize employees of the 94 U.S. Attorney’s Offices nationwide who have distinguished themselves through extraordinary professional achievements and excellence. The Northern District of Georgia personnel were recognized for Superior Performance by a Litigation Team and Superior Performance by an Administrative Team.

Superior Performance by a Litigation Team

(From left to right: Acting Deputy Attorney General R. Trent McCotter, Child Victim Witness Program Administrator Nicole E. Borrello, Army Criminal Investigation Division Special Agent Bryce T. Wolford, FBI Special Agent Will M. Mauk, FBI Unit Chief Johanna M. Norman, EOUSA Director Francey Hakes, Trial Attorney Eduardo A. Layton, were recognized alongside partners from the Justice Department’s Criminal Division, the Federal Bureau of Investigation, and the Department of the Army Criminal Investigation Division for the successful prosecution of Edward Zappey, a child predator and former elementary school teacher who was sentenced to life imprisonment without the possibility of parole after sexually abusing four students on an American military base in Germany nearly 20 years ago. BOSTON – A member of the violent Boston-based gang, H-Block, has pleaded guilty in federal court in Boston to drug conspiracy charges. Defendant is currently an inmate at a state correctional facility where he smuggled illegal drugs into the prison.

Timothy Hearns, a/k/a “King Kill,” a/k/a “Tooly,” a/k/a “Toolman,” 36, of Roxbury; pleaded guilty on Oct. 30, 2026 to conspiracy to distribute and to possess with intent to distribute PCP, MDMB-4en-PINACA and ADB-4en-PINACA. U.S. District Court Judge Indira Talwani scheduled sentencing for Feb. 2, 2027.

Hearns was one of 10 H-Block gang members and associates charged in August 2024 following a multi-year investigation of H-Block beginning in 2021 in response to an uptick in gang-related drug trafficking, shootings and violence. According to court documents, over 500 grams of cocaine, cocaine base (crack cocaine) and fentanyl, as well as over 20,000 doses of drug-laced paper were seized during the investigation.

According to the charging documents, the H-Block street gang is one of the most feared and influential city-wide gangs in Boston. Originally formed in the 1980s as the Humboldt Raiders in the Roxbury section of Boston, the gang re-emerged in the 2000s as H-Block. Current members of H-Block have a history of violent confrontation with law enforcement, including an incident in 2015 when a member shot a Boston Police officer at point blank range without warning or provocation.

Hearns is an inmate at a state correctional institution, currently serving a 19.5 to 20-year manslaughter sentence in the Massachusetts Department of Correction. Hearns was sentenced in 2014 for committing a 2010 shooting that killed a 14-year-old at the Columbus/Heath Street basketball courts, during a time when he and other members of H-Block were engaged in a violent rivalry with Heath Street gang associates. A 15-year-old boy was also shot and struck in the chest and arm but survived.

Hearns is a long-time H-Block gang member and one of three members and associates charged with conspiring to smuggle illegal drugs into a Massachusetts prison. According to court documents, the Massachusetts Department of Correction has seen a significant increase in the smuggling of synthetic cannabinoids, a/k/a “K2,” and other dangerous substances into the prison system. A common method of introducing the drugs is by exploiting the Department of Correction’s inmate mail policies, which prohibit delivery to inmates of original copies of any materials contained in incoming mail except for legal mail, original copies of which are inspected and delivered via the U.S. postal system. Sheets of paper are saturated or sprayed with liquid narcotics, dried, printed with fake legal correspondence, and then mailed to inmates in an envelope marked as legal mail, in the hope that the drug-laced paper will be delivered undetected. It is alleged that several sheets of paper containing PCP (Phenylcyclidine) and illegal K2 were seized over the course of the investigation. It is estimated that a single sheet of such paper would be worth as much as $80,000 inside the prison. Intercepted jail calls revealed that Hearns along with his co-conspirators, conspired to introduce synthetic drugs into the facilities. Hearns is the 10th and final defendant to plead guilty in the case.

The charges of conspiracy to distribute and to possess with intent to distribute PCP, MDMB-4en-PINACA and ADB-4en-PINACA provides for a sentence of up to 20 years in prison, at least three years and up to a lifetime of supervised release and a fine of up to $1 million. Sentences are imposed by a federal district court judge based upon the U.S. Sentencing Guidelines and statutes which govern the determination of a sentence in a criminal case. United States Attorney Leah B. Foley; Jarod A. Forget, Special Agent in Charge of the Drug Enforcement Administration, New England Field Division; Special Agent in Charge Mark Comorosky of the U.S. Secret Service Boston Field Office; Ted. E. Docks, Special Agent in Charge of the Federal Bureau of Investigation, Boston Division; Boston Police Commissioner Michael Cox; and Anthony D’Esposito, Inspector General, U.S. Department of Labor, Office of Inspector General made the announcement. The investigation was supported by the Massachusetts State Police; Suffolk County District Attorney’s Office; Massachusetts Department of Corrections; and the Braintree, Quincy, Randolph and Watertown Police Departments. Assistant United States Attorney John T. Dawley of the Organized Crime & Gang Unit is prosecuting the cases.

This case is part of the Homeland Security Task Force (HSTF) initiative established by Executive Order 14159, Protecting the American People Against Invasion. The HSTF is a whole-of-government partnership dedicated to eliminating criminal cartels, foreign gangs, transnational criminal organizations, and human smuggling and trafficking rings operating in the United States and abroad. Through historic interagency collaboration, the HSTF directs the full might of United States law enforcement towards identifying, investigating, and prosecuting the full spectrum of crimes committed by these organizations, which have long fueled violence and instability within our borders. In performing this work, the HSTF places special emphasis on investigating and prosecuting those engaged in child trafficking or other crimes involving children. The HSTF further utilizes all available tools to prosecute and remove the most violent criminal aliens from the United States. HSTF Boston comprises agents and officers from HSI, FBI, DEA, ATF, USMS, IRS-CI, USPIS, DOL-OIG and DSS, as well as several state and local law enforcement agencies, with the prosecution being led by the United States Attorney’s Office for the District of Massachusetts.

Gainesville, Florida – Pablo Gomez-Sarmiento, 25, of Mexico, was sentenced to the statutory maximum sentence of two years in federal prison after pleading guilty to illegal reentry into the United States. The sentence was announced by John P. Heekin, United States Attorney for the Northern District of Florida.

U.S. Attorney Heekin said: “This case reaffirms the absolute necessity of securing our borders against criminal illegal aliens and aggressively enforcing our immigration laws. The defendant’s rape of the child in the underlying state case was 100% preventable. That heartbreaking case is the precise reason why President Donald J. Trump and Attorney General Todd Blanche have committed the Department of Justice to repelling the invasion of illegal immigration that took place under the prior administration, to ensure we keep criminal illegal aliens, like this defendant, out of our country.”

Court documents reflect that the defendant, a citizen of Mexico, was removed from the United States in January 2020. Thereafter, the defendant unlawfully returned to the United States, and he was arrested in Alachua County, Florida, in 2024 for impregnating a child under the age of 16. The Defendant admitted to observing the 15-year-old victim getting off a school bus and was aware that she was under 18 years old. He was convicted in 2025 and sentenced to state prison. While the defendant was serving his state sentence, the United States Immigration and Custom’s Enforcement became aware of the defendant’s presence in the United States and initiated the federal criminal charge.

“Criminal illegal aliens who prey on children will find no place to hide from the women and men of ICE” said ICE Enforcement and Removal Operations Miami Field Office Director Matthew Elliston. “This criminal alien unlawfully returned to the United States after removal and then targeted a child to sexually exploit. ICE will not tolerate those who defy our immigration laws and prey on innocent victims.”

The case was investigated by U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement’s Enforcement and Removal Operations and the Gainesville Police Department. Assistant United States Attorney Tyler Fleming prosecuted the case.

This case is part of Operation Take Back America, a nationwide initiative that marshals the full resources of the Department of Justice to repel the invasion of illegal immigration, achieve the total elimination of cartels and transnational criminal organizations (TCOs), and protect our communities from the perpetrators of violent crime.

The United States Attorney’s Office for the Northern District of Florida is one of 94 offices that serve as the nation’s principal litigators under the direction of the Attorney General. Release Number 9319-26
CFTC Chairman Selig Releases Statement on Equity Perpetual Futures
November 03, 2026
WASHINGTON — CFTC Chairman Michael S. Selig today released a statement announcing that perpetual futures contracts on individual equity securities can begin trading for the first time on designated contract markets that are dually registered with the Securities and Exchange Commission as notice-registered national securities exchanges to trade security futures products.
Key excerpts from Chairman Selig’s statement:
“Today, perpetual futures contracts on individual equity securities (the ‘Equity Perps’) can begin trading for the first time on CFTC-registered exchanges.
…
“This expansion marks a significant step towards allowing U.S. market participants, consistent with applicable law, to avail themselves of the advantages of perpetual futures that have led to their emergence as widely sought tools for risk-management and price-discovery. I believe that bringing these types of innovative products into our regulated markets ensures that American investors and traders can access these products within the protections of the CFTC’s proven regulatory framework, rather than being forced to turn to offshore, and often unregulated, venues.
…
“The Equity Perps build on the foundation of the [Commodity Futures Modernization Act of 2000] and the [CFTC-SEC Memorandum of Understanding]. For too long, regulatory uncertainty left innovative products, such as security futures and equity perpetual futures, stranded in what SEC Chairman Paul S. Atkins has aptly described as a regulatory ‘no man’s land’ due to a lack of harmonization between the agencies. The CFTC and SEC have turned the page on that era, and are committed to delivering regulatory clarity for innovative products and a clear path to market, rather than more casualties of jurisdictional disputes.”
Read Chairman Selig’s full statement here.
-CFTC-
title: CFTC Chairman Selig Releases Statement on Equity Perpetual Futures

SAGAMIHARA, Japan — Firefighters from U.S. Army Garrison Japan participated in the annual Comprehensive Disaster Preparedness Drill Oct. 25 at a joint-use area here near Sagami General Depot.
The multi-agency event brought diverse organizations together to tackle realistic emergency scenarios following a major earthquake.
During the exercise, teams responded to a simulated collapsed building to rescue two trapped victims. After a rescue dog pinpointed their location, firefighters breached the roof and deployed a ladder crane to safely extract an unconscious individual.
Ichiro Otsuka, a fire truck driver and operator assigned to USAG Japan, highlighted the value of joint operations.
“Practice doesn’t lie,” Otsuka said, emphasizing the continuous reflection and daily communication that prepared the team.
Otsuka praised the dedication of the Sagamihara firefighters, adding, “Their eyes shone with pride in protecting citizens’ lives and property. Working together gave us great motivation and exposed us to new tactical approaches and equipment.”
Acknowledging that room for improvement remains, Otsuka reaffirmed the two groups’ shared commitment to learning from one another and working tirelessly to safeguard the community.

Advance ticket reservations secure guaranteed seats and the best fares
WASHINGTON – As Thanksgiving approaches, Amtrak is encouraging travelers to book early to secure the best fares and guaranteed seats, as tickets are selling quickly. Thanksgiving is Amtrak’s busiest travel season and one of the busiest travel periods nationwide. In 2025, Amtrak broke ridership records during the Thanksgiving holiday with more than 1.2 million customer trips—a nearly 6% increase from 2024. Amtrak predicts another year of record ridership this holiday season and recommends travelers plan their trips early.
“Amtrak is experiencing record demand, a testament to the comfortable and convenient experience of traveling by train,” said Amtrak Interim President Byl Herrmann. “We are honored to help customers reach their holiday destinations safely and comfortably, while offering more departures, amenities and services during a time when they appreciate them most.”
Train travel offers many benefits: no waiting in long airport lines, a quick and easy boarding process, no roadway traffic, and arrival downtown, where connecting travel options are abundant.
To help accommodate the expected surge of customers during Thanksgiving week, Amtrak is expanding capacity by adding cars to select Northeast Regional trains from Nov. 20-30. Two additional Northeast Regional round trips will be added with service between Washington Union Station, New York Penn Station, and cities in between on Nov. 24-25 and Nov. 28-29. With record demand, this additional capacity is expected to fill quickly.

ICE HSI Chattanooga busts 2 foreign nationals accused of voting illegally in 2024 election
CHATANOOGA — ICE’s Homeland Security Investigations agents arrested Frederic Jean Rene Sicard, a French national, and Mark Adwar Odisho, an Iraqi national, in Cleveland Oct. 29. Both foreign nationals were charged with voting by aliens in violation of U.S. law and both are believed to have committed voter fraud during the 2024 presidential election.
“Election security is national security,” said ICE Assistant Director of Public Affairs Micah Bock. “When foreign nationals allegedly cast ballots in our elections, they undermine the integrity of the democratic process and the rights of lawful voters. Our election laws are not optional, and ICE will work with our law enforcement partners to investigate violations and hold offenders accountable.”
Under President Trump, Secretary Mullin and acting ICE Director David J. Venturella’s leadership, ICE is once again focused on enforcing the law, protecting the public and removing dangerous individuals from our communities.
HSI Chattanooga undertook the arrest as part of a joint investigation with the FBI and with assistance from the Cleveland Police Department. The Eastern District of Tennessee issued a criminal complaint and arrest warrant against the subjects Oct. 23.
This investigation reflects HSI Chattanooga’s continued commitment to protecting the integrity of the nation’s electoral process through coordination with federal, state and local law enforcement partners.

Stakeholders Are Encouraged to Review Notice of Proposed Rulemaking and Submit Comments
Alexandria, VA (November 03, 2026) ― The National Credit Union Administration today announced two final rules and a proposed rule as part of the fourteenth round of proposed regulatory changes associated with NCUA’s Deregulation Project. The project is an ongoing review of NCUA’s regulations to ensure they are focused on credit unions’ safety, soundness, and resilience. With today’s announcement, NCUA is requesting comments on one proposal that would eliminate an obsolete regulation in the Code of Federal Regulations.
The proposal includes:
NPRM Summary
The NCUA Board (Board) is seeking public comments on an interim final rule that removes 12 CFR 723.9, an outdated transitional provision in the commercial lending regulation. The provision was adopted as part of the 2016 commercial lending rule to address credit unions operating under certain NCUA-approved waivers or supervisory actions during the transition to a principles-based regulatory framework. The Board has determined that the provision has served its purpose and is no longer necessary. Removing it would reduce regulatory complexity and improve the clarity of NCUA's regulations.
The two final rules NCUA announced are:
The Board adopted a final rule that makes permanent the regulatory treatment of Paycheck Protection Program (PPP) loans that have been in place since April 27, 2020. These provisions were originally adopted during the COVID-19 pandemic to implement the Coronavirus Aid, Relief, and Economic Security Act (CARES Act).
The Board also amended 12 CFR 701.39 by removing paragraph (a)(1), which defined the phrase "except as otherwise provided by law or except as otherwise provided by federal law." The Board determined that the definition was unnecessary because credit unions are already responsible for identifying and complying with applicable laws when exercising their statutory lien authority. This change does not affect a credit union's statutory lien authority or existing legal obligations.
Find a detailed summary for each proposal at https://ncua.gov/news/deregulation-project/.
To submit comments, type or paste the docket numbers into the search on the Federal Rulemaking Portal.
title: NCUA Announces Fourteenth Round of Deregulation Proposals

text:
DOJ To Monitor Elections in All 50 States for First Time
One of the Department of Justice’s (DOJ) most important missions is ensuring election integrity, supporting free and fair elections, and protecting the right to vote for U.S. citizens across the United States. The DOJ has sent election monitors in support of this mission since the enactment of the Voting Rights Act in 1965 across all Administrations.
Today, the DOJ will further this mission by engaging in its largest monitoring effort in history—with approximately 1,000 election monitors and observers deployed, and, for the first time, in all 50 states. The effort is coordinated by the Civil Rights Division. Monitors will include personnel from the Division, other DOJ divisions/components, U.S. Attorney’s Offices and federal observers from the Office of Personnel Management. Throughout Election Day, Division personnel will maintain contact with state and local election officials.
“Election integrity has been one of the top priorities for this Administration and this Division,” said Assistant Attorney General Harmeet K. Dhillon of the Civil Rights Division at the Department of Justice. “I am very proud we are deploying the largest monitoring effort in DOJ history, and pursuing transparency for elections in an assertive and nondiscriminatory manner.”
Election monitors will be checking for compliance with the federal voting rights statutes that fall within the jurisdiction of the Division. The Division’s Voting Section enforces the civil provisions of federal statutes that protect the right to vote, including the Voting Rights Act, National Voter Registration Act, Help America Vote Act, Uniformed and Overseas Citizens Absentee Voting Act, and Civil Rights Acts.
The Division’s Disability Rights Section enforces the Americans with Disabilities Act (ADA) to ensure that persons with disabilities have a full and equal opportunity to vote. The Division’s Criminal Section enforces federal criminal statutes that prohibit voter intimidation and voter suppression based on race, color, national origin, or religion.
Throughout the day and week, Division personnel will be available to receive questions and complaints from the public related to federal voting rights laws. If you have a question or complaint, please call our election issues hotline at 1-800-253-3931, email us at VEM@usdoj.gov, or submit a complaint through our website at www.civilrights.justice.gov/report.
Individuals with questions or complaints related to the ADA may call the Division’s toll-free ADA information hotline at 1-800-514-0301 or 1-833-610-1264 (TTY) or submit a complaint through our ADA website at www.ada.gov.
Complaints related to any disruptions at a polling place should always be reported to local election officials (including officials based in the polling place). Complaints related to violence, threats of violence or intimidation at a polling place should be reported immediately to local police authorities by calling 911. These complaints should also be reported to the department after local authorities have been contacted.
To learn more about what the DOJ and the Civil Rights Division has done historically to protect the vote and ensure free and fair elections, go to www.civilrights.justice.gov/electionintegrity.

BOSTON – A Dominican man unlawfully residing in Lynn was indicted by a federal grand jury for unlawfully reentering the United States after deportation.

Cesar Fernando Guerrero-Casado, 41, was indicted for illegally reentering the United States after deportation. The defendant is currently detained in state custody on unrelated charges and appeared in federal court on Nov. 2, 2026.

According to the indictment, Guerrero-Casado was previously removed from the United States on Feb. 24, 2015. It is alleged that sometime after his February 2015 removal, Guerrero-Casado illegally reentered the United States without permission.

Guerrero-Casado was previously convicted of unlawful reentry in 2014. He is currently serving state prison sentences for drug offenses.

The charge of unlawful reentry of a deported alien provides for a sentence of up to 10 years in prison, three years of supervised release and a fine of up to $250,000. The defendant is subject to deportation upon completion of any sentence imposed. Sentences are imposed by a federal district court judge based upon the U.S. Sentencing Guidelines and statutes which govern the determination of a sentence in a criminal case.

United States Attorney Leah B. Foley and David T. Wesling, Acting Field Office Director of U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement’s Enforcement and Removal Operations in Boston made the announcement. Assistant U.S. Attorney Catherine Conroy of the Major Crimes Unit is prosecuting the case.

The details contained in the charging document are allegations. The defendant is presumed to be innocent unless and until proven guilty beyond a reasonable doubt in the court of law.
title: Illegal Alien from Dominican Republic Indicted for Unlawful Reentry

EPA Enforcement Leadership Helps Promote Military Readiness and Participates in Training During Swing Through Wyoming and Colorado
WASHINGTON – U.S. Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) Assistant Administrator for Enforcement and Compliance Assurance Jeffrey A. Hall and Principal Deputy Craig Pritzlaff recently visited Wyoming and Colorado to promote military readiness and focus criminal environmental enforcement on major federal cases. In Wyoming, they visited a Minuteman launch control center and missile silo to understand the challenges the Air Force Global Strike Command faces in keeping missileers safe in aging missile facilities and to provide assistance in achieving compliance with indoor environmental standards. In Colorado, they participated in EPA’s criminal enforcement attorneys’ biannual training program, speaking on this Administration’s focus on federal priorities, including using the environmental laws to protect against foreign toxins.
“We are keeping the airmen stationed in missile alert facilities safe by helping the Air Force comply with toxic substances regulations, and that allows our warfighters to focus on defending our country,” said Assistant Administrator Hall.
Assistant Administrator Hall visited F.E. Warren Air Force Base, home of the Twentieth Air Force, which is responsible for U.S. intercontinental ballistic missiles, as part of EPA’s commitment to partner with the Department of War (DoW). The visit was focused on the Air Force’s ongoing efforts to comply with the nation’s environmental laws, address environmental hazards, and protect the homeland.
“Our highest priority for our criminal program is that it holds the worst environmental criminals accountable while being true to the Constitution and the rule of law,” said Assistant Administrator Hall. “EPA’s criminal enforcement attorneys ensure that our criminal program can investigate and prosecute cases effectively and lawfully.”
In support of Administrator Zeldin’s Powering the Great American Comeback initiative, the biannual training conference highlighted EPA’s effort to protect Americans by pursuing those who intentionally pollute or profit from sending harmful products and chemicals into the United States. The training program teaches EPA’s criminal enforcement attorneys about new developments in the investigation and prosecution of environmental crimes and fosters a collaborative working relationship. The training program focused on enforcement initiatives, civil and criminal coordination, 4th Amendment issues, trial strategies, and significant appellate decisions.
title: EPA Enforcement Leadership Helps Promote Military Readiness and Participates in Training During Swing Through Wyoming and Colorado

GREAT FALLS – A Browning man who strangled one girlfriend and beat another almost to death was sentenced today to five years in prison, followed by three years of supervised release, U.S. Attorney Scott Twito said.

Jeremiah James Harwood, 23, pleaded guilty under a global plea agreement in August 2026 to three charges from two separate cases: strangulation, assault resulting in serious bodily injury, and witness tampering.

Chief U.S. District Judge Brian M. Morris presided.

The government alleged in court documents that Harwood strangled one intimate partner and beat another almost to death. After beating his partner, he then tried to convince her to change her testimony against him.

Harwood strangled his first partner using a lanyard she was wearing. The two were fighting and Harwood tackled the victim while trying to take her phone. He then grabbed the lanyard she had around her neck and began to choke her until she couldn’t breathe. At that point she stopped resisting and Harwood let go.

Roughly a year later, while on pretrial release for the strangulation charge, Harwood was in a new relationship with a different partner. Harwood attacked that partner on two occasions about two weeks apart, each time sending her to the hospital with significant head injuries. After the second assault, his partner was diagnosed with a traumatic brain injury that required intubation and surgery.

Law enforcement began an investigation after the assault, at which point Harwood reached out to the victim and attempted to convince her to redo her statement and tell investigators he was not involved. Instead, she reported him to the FBI.

The U.S. Attorney’s Office prosecuted the case. The Blackfeet Law Enforcement Services and the FBI conducted the investigation.
title: Browning man sentenced to five years in prison for strangling one victim, beating another, and witness tampering

Statement from U.S. Attorney’s Office and DEA El Paso Division

ALBUQUERQUE – An Albuquerque woman is facing federal drug trafficking and firearm offenses after an HSTF investigation allegedly recovered large quantities of fentanyl, heroin, cash, and firearms from her Albuquerque residence.

According to court documents, law enforcement is investigating a drug trafficking organization allegedly importing large quantities of fentanyl, heroin and other narcotics into Albuquerque, New Mexico. On October 28, 2026, a U.S. Magistrate Judge authorized a federal search warrant for the residence of Angel Ramirez , 45, in northwest Albuquerque.

On October 29, 2026, agents executed the warrant and encountered Ramirez , the sole adult in the home. Inside the master bedroom, investigators allegedly located multiple duffel bags containing large quantities of narcotics, bulk U.S. currency, and numerous firearms. Laboratory field testing confirmed the presence of fentanyl and heroin.

In total, agents recovered approximately 43.75 kilograms of fentanyl powder, the largest seizure in New Mexico in the DEA history, 7.70 kilograms of fentanyl pills, 4.40 kilograms of heroin, and an additional 1,036 grams of fentanyl in a separate container. Investigators also located approximately 29 firearms and assorted ammunition inside and around a gun safe directly beneath the narcotics and cash.

Court documents state that Ramirez was employed as a paralegal with the State of New Mexico’s Department of Justice, a taxpayer‑funded position of public trust. Investigators allege that Ramirez leveraged her government employment, clean criminal history, and internal access to the justice system to create a veneer of legitimacy while her residence operated as a distribution hub for narcotics, drug proceeds, and firearms.

“Nearly 50 kilograms of fentanyl powder in a single Albuquerque home tells us just how serious the drug trafficking problem has become in New Mexico,” said First Assistant U.S. Attorney Ryan Ellison. “This is a tremendous accomplishment by the agents who got these drugs off our streets, but it is no cause for celebration. With fentanyl overdose deaths on the rise in New Mexico, we have a lot more work to do. We will continue targeting the organizations bringing these drugs into our state and aggressively prosecuting those responsible.”

With fentanyl overdose deaths on the rise in New Mexico, we have a lot more work to do. We will continue targeting the organizations bringing these drugs into our state and aggressively prosecuting those responsible.”

“As members of the community, I want you to know that our agents remain deeply committed to protecting and serving the city of Albuquerque,” said DEA El Paso Division Special Agent in Charge Robert “Eric” Castañeda. “I’m proud of their professionalism, dedication, and the outstanding work they demonstrated throughout this operation. DEA remains steadfast in our mission to keep our communities safe.”

“As members of the community, I want you to know that our agents remain deeply committed to protecting and serving the city of Albuquerque,” said DEA El Paso Division Special Agent in Charge Robert “Eric” Castañeda. “I’m proud of their professionalism, dedication, and the outstanding work they demonstrated throughout this operation. DEA remains steadfast in our mission to keep our communities safe.”

Ramirez is charged with possession with intent to distribute fentanyl and using and carrying a firearm during and in relation to a drug trafficking crime. She will remain in custody pending trial which has not been scheduled. If convicted of the current charges, Ramirez faces no less than 15 years and up to life in prison.

First Assistant U.S. Attorney Ryan Ellison made the announcement today on behalf of HSTF. Assistant U.S. Attorneys Mark Probasco, Timothy Piatt and Oliver Stephanz are prosecuting the case.

This arrest is part of the Homeland Security Task Force (HSTF) initiative established by Executive Order 14159, Protecting the American People Against Invasion. The HSTF is a whole-of-government partnership dedicated to eliminating criminal cartels, foreign gangs, transnational criminal organizations, and human smuggling and trafficking rings operating in the United States and abroad. Through historic interagency collaboration, the HSTF directs the full might of United States law enforcement towards identifying, investigating, and prosecuting the full spectrum of crimes committed by these organizations, which have long fueled violence and instability within our borders. In performing this work, the HSTF places special emphasis on investigating and prosecuting those engaged in child trafficking or other crimes involving children. The HSTF further utilizes all available tools to prosecute and remove the most violent criminal aliens from the United States.

HSTF Region II CORE 7 is comprised of agents and officers from Homeland Security Investigations (HSI), the Federal Bureau of Investigations (FBI), the Drug Enforcement Administration (DEA), Bureau of Alcohol, Tobacco, Firearms and Explosives (ATF), Internal Revenue Service Criminal Investigation (IRS-CI), Customs and Border Protection – Office of Field Operations (OFO), U.S. Border Patrol (USBP) and Air and Marine (AMO), Office of Professional Responsibility (OPR), United States Department of the Interior – Bureau of Land Management (BLM), Joint Task Force North (JTF-N), United States Postal Inspection Service (USPIS), United States Marshal Service (USMS), Department of State, Bureau of Diplomatic Security (DSS), U.S. Citizenship and Immigration Services (USCIS), Texas Department of Public Safety (TXDPS), El Paso Police Department (EPPD), New Mexico State Police (NMSP), West Texas / New Mexico High Intensity Drug Trafficking Areas (HIDTA), Albuquerque Police Department, New Mexico Sixth Judicial District, Las Cruces/Dona Ana County Metro Narcotics Agency, and the prosecution is being led by the Office of the United States Attorney for the Districts of Western Texas and New Mexico.

The Sandoval County Sheriff’s Office, Bernalillo County Sheriff’s Office, Rio Rancho Police Department and Pueblo of Pojoaque Tribal Police Department provided invaluable assistance in this arrest.

Robert Bowers, Senior Inspector
NORFOLK, Virginia – A fugitive investigation that spanned several states and lasted over 18 months came to an end today when the U. S. Marshals Service (USMS) arrested a fugitive who was wanted in relation to a homicide that occurred in Hampton on April 11, 2025.
The USMS Capital Area Regional Fugitive Task Force (CARFTF), in conjunction with the USMS New York/New Jersey Regional Fugitive Task Force arrested Curtis Shermaine Frazier, Jr., 27, shortly after 9:30 a.m., in the 5000 block of Farragut Avenue in Brooklyn, New York. Frazier was wanted on charges of second-degree murder, use of a firearm in the commission of a felony, shooting in a public place, and reckless handling of a firearm.
All charges were related to a Hampton homicide at the Karma Lounge that took the life of 25-year-old D’Angelo Osborne.
Shortly after the homicide, investigators with the Hampton Police Division requested assistance from the USMS Capital Area Regional Fugitive Task Force with locating and apprehending Frazier. The USMS CARFTF followed up on leads in North Carolina and Georgia before ultimately apprehending Frazier in New York.
Frazier was arrested without incident and is being held at Brooklyn Central Booking, where he will await extradition to Virginia to face charges.
The USMS Capital Area Regional Fugitive Task Force was established in June of 2004, has partnership agreements with over 100 federal, state, and local agencies and has 8 fully operational offices. To date, the USMS CARFTF has arrested more than 111,488 fugitives.
