Foreign Military Sales: Congressional Notification

Bureau of Political-Military Affairs

November 2, 2026

Transmittal #26-95

The U.S. Department of State has made a determination approving a possible Foreign Military Sale to the Government of Jordan for Advanced Precision Kill Weapon System II and related equipment. The estimated total cost is $100 million.

The Government of Jordan has requested to buy up to one thousand five hundred (1,500) WGU-59A/B or B/B Single Variant Block Upgrade (air-to-air, ground-to-air, or air-to-ground) Advanced Precision Kill Weapon System II (All-up-rounds or guidance sections). The following non-major defense equipment items will also be included: launchers; Mk-152 high explosive warheads; MK66 rocket motors; proximity fuzes; WTU-1/B practice warheads; inert MK66 rocket motors; support equipment; publications and technical documentation; transportation; U.S. Government and contractor engineering, technical, training, and logistical support services; and other related elements of logistics and program support. The estimated total cost is $100 million.

This proposed sale will support the foreign policy and national security objectives of the United States by helping to improve the security of a Major Non-NATO Ally that is an important force for political stability and economic progress in the Middle East.

The proposed sale will improve Jordan’s capability to meet current and future threats by providing enhancement to its air defense capability in support of the Middle East Air Defense pillar of the Regional Security Construct. The acquisition of additional APKWS II guided rockets will increase Jordan’s capacity to defend itself, allow for the reduction of sustained U.S. support over time, and provide increased security for U.S. military assets stationed in Jordan. Jordan will have no difficulty absorbing these articles and services into its armed forces.

The proposed sale of this equipment and support will not alter the basic military balance in the region.

The principal contractor will be BAE Systems, Inc., located in Nashua, NH. At this time, the U.S. Government is not aware of any offset agreement proposed in connection with this potential sale. Any offset agreement will be defined in negotiations between the purchaser and the contractor.

Implementation of this proposed sale will not require the assignment of any additional U.S. Government or contractor representatives to Jordan. Only additional periodic participation in program and technical reviews, training, and maintenance support will be required.

There will be no adverse impact on U.S. defense readiness as a result of this proposed sale.

For further information, please contact the Bureau of Political-Military Affairs Outreach Team at T_Outreach_PM@State.gov .

HUNTINGTON, W.Va. – Anton Marcel Jeffries, 32, of Akron, Ohio, was sentenced to one year and nine months in prison, to be followed by four years of supervised release, for violating supervised release.

According to court documents and statements made in court, September 18, 2025, Jeffries was arrested and charged with intent to deliver a controlled substance in Kanawha County Magistrate Court. Jeffries was arrested after law enforcement officers investigated the source of a significant increase in drug overdoses in Charleston between September 17 and September 18, 2025. Jeffries pleaded guilty to possession of a controlled substance, fentanyl, in Kanawha County Circuit Court on September 14, 2026.

At the time of this offense, Jeffries was serving a term of supervised release following his conviction for possession with intent to distribute methamphetamine, heroin, and fentanyl in United States District Court for the Southern District of West Virginia on August 27, 2019. Jeffries began his term of supervised release on September 12, 2025, six days before his arrest.

United States District Judge Robert C. Chambers revoked Jeffries’ supervised release and imposed the sentence, to be served consecutively to his state sentence, following a hearing on October 26, 2026. Assistant United States Attorney Sarah N. Hudson prosecuted the case.

United States Attorney Moore Capito made the announcement and commended the investigative work of the Charleston Police Department.

U.S. Coast Guard Awards $114 Million Contract to Modernize Critical Water Infrastructure at Base Kodiak, Bolstering Arctic Readiness
WASHINGTON — The U.S. Coast Guard awarded a $114 million contract on Oct. 29, 2026 to Gilbane Federal of Providence, Rhode Island, to modernize the water distribution system at Base Kodiak, Alaska. Funded through the One Big Beautiful Bill Act, this project directly strengthens operational readiness and quality of life at the Coast Guard’s largest operational installation.
As a vital hub for projecting U.S. presence and defending national sovereignty across Alaska and the Arctic approaches, Base Kodiak supports surface and aviation operations in a demanding maritime environment. The contract encompasses all design, labor, material, equipment, and site work necessary to deliver a resilient, modern water utility network, with completion scheduled for Oct. 2031.
Project Key Highlights:
- System Recapitalization: Replaces and upgrades more than 8 miles of main water distribution lines across Base Kodiak.
- Storage Capacity: Replaces four large-scale water storage tanks critical to base operations.
- Aviation and Facility Fire Suppression: Delivers dedicated water supply and pressure reliability for fire suppression systems protecting two operational aircraft hangars and key shore facilities.
- Workforce Quality of Life: Ensures safe, dependable potable water for the active-duty, reserve, civilian, and family members living and working on base.
- Execution and Oversight: Civil Engineering Unit (CEU) Juneau is executing this project, operating under the Shore Infrastructure Logistics Center within the Coast Guard’s Program Executive Office (PEO) Shore.
“Every day, the Coast Guard delivers value to our Nation by controlling, securing, and defending our northern border and maritime approaches in the Arctic,” said Rear Adm. Jon Hickey, Deputy Commandant for Systems. “Our crews need modern, resilient shore capabilities to answer the call and get the mission done. By investing $114 million to modernize Base Kodiak’s critical water and fire-suppression infrastructure, we are directly supporting our forces and their families while building the foundation for our expanding polar fleet and long-term mission readiness.”
Driving Holistic Arctic Transformation
Base Kodiak is central to the Coast Guard’s strategic posture in the high latitudes and designated as the future homeport for the Service’s first two Arctic Security Cutters. The water distribution modernization complements a comprehensive suite of infrastructure projects currently planned or underway at Base Kodiak to support expanding mission capabilities and workforce growth, including:
- Construction of a new fuel pier and upgrades to the cargo wharf to support major cutters and icebreakers.
- Construction of 30 additional family housing units and a new child development center to support Coast Guard personnel and their families.
Using the nearly $25 billion investment in the One Big Beautiful Bill Act, the largest capital investment in the Service’s history, the Coast Guard has already ordered over $20 billion in new assets and capabilities, critical depot maintenance, and shore facilities. This rapid investment demonstrates the Coast Guard’s commitment to modernizing acquisition, delivering next-generation technology, restoring readiness, and revitalizing shore infrastructure.
For media inquiries contact mediarelations@uscg.mil.
###
About the U.S. Coast Guard 
With more than 95,000 miles of shoreline, 25,000 miles of navigable rivers and 4.5 million square miles of U.S. exclusive economic zone, the U.S. Coast Guard defends the Nation, protects the marine transportation system, regulates and safeguards ports and waterways, leads the Nation in maritime drug interdiction and secures the maritime border. As a member of the joint force, a law enforcement organization, a regulatory agency and a member of the U.S. intelligence community, the Coast Guard employs a unique mix of authorities to ensure the safety and integrity of the maritime domain to protect the economic and national security of the nation. More than 76,000 members of the Coast Guard operate a multi-mission, interoperable fleet of more than 220 cutters, 185 fixed and rotary-wing aircraft, 1,300 boats and its own dedicated cyber command to protect critical maritime infrastructure.
More information about the U.S. Coast Guard can be found at www.uscg.mil Follow @USCG on X and Instagram, like us on Facebook, subscribe on YouTube and follow LinkedIn—connect with us.
Make a difference on land, at sea or in the air with the Coast Guard. Visit GoCoastGuard.com to find out how to be part of our team.

Gainesville, Florida – Kensha Eugene Williams, 26, of Gainesville, Florida, has pleaded guilty in federal court on a charge of possession of a firearm and ammunition by a convicted felon. John P. Heekin, United States Attorney for the Northern District of Florida announced the guilty plea.

U.S. Attorney Heekin said: “Our state and federal law enforcement officers work hard every day to keep our citizens safe from dangerous, violent felons, like this defendant, and I am proud to back up their hard work with successful prosecutions like this one.”

According to court records, on June 28, 2026, law enforcement observed the defendant in possession of a suspected drugs. Once detained and searched, the officer located a firearm and ammunition in the defendant’s pocket. The defendant has prior convictions for Aggravated Assault with Firearm and Carrying a Concealed Firearm and therefore cannot legally possess a firearm and ammunition.

Sentencing is scheduled for February 16, 2027, at 2:30pm before Chief United States District Court Judge Allen Winsor in Gainesville, Florida. The Defendant faces up to 15 years’ imprisonment.

The case was jointly investigated by the Bureau of Alcohol, Tobacco, Firearms and Explosives and the Gainesville Police Department. The case is being prosecuted by Assistant United States Attorney Tyler Fleming.

Project Safe Neighborhoods (PSN) is the Department of Justice’s nationwide initiative that brings federal, state, local, and tribal law enforcement, prosecutors, and other public safety partners together to coordinate efforts to combat violent crime and make communities safe. Coordinated by U.S. Attorneys’ offices in each of the 94 federal districts, PSN is tailored to particular communities to strategically address specific violent crime and public safety challenges. As a key component of Operation Take Back America, PSN serves a central role in the Department’s commitment to make our country safe. PSN emphasizes three core principles: rapid federal response to violent crime and criminal offenders; strong, strategic partnerships among law enforcement at all levels; and accountability and deterrence through the prosecution of the most serious, readily provable offenses and other strategies. These efforts complement and strengthen President Trump’s Homeland Security Task Forces, ensuring a comprehensive federal response to the most pressing public safety issues facing communities .

The United States Attorney’s Office for the Northern District of Florida is one of 94 offices that serve as the nation’s principal litigators under the direction of the Attorney General. To access public court documents online, please visit the U.S. District Court for the Northern District of Florida website. For more information about the United States Attorney’s Office, Northern District of Florida, visit https://www.justice.gov/usao-ndfl .

ALEXANDRIA, Va. – A Venezuelan national who resided in Miami was sentenced today to 12 years in prison for conspiracy to launder money. Jorge Figueira, 60, laundered billions of dollars for numerous and varied illicit actors, including drug trafficking organizations. Figueira also agreed to a $1 billion money judgment.

According to court documents, the laundering network of Figueira used various bank accounts, cryptocurrency exchange accounts, private cryptocurrency wallets, and shell companies to launder voluminous amounts of illicit money into and out of the United States. Figueira used a series of steps, including the conversion of money to cryptocurrency that was directed to a series of digital wallets. Figueira would send the funds to liquidity providers to exchange the cryptocurrency for dollars, then transfer the dollars to Figueira's bank accounts and ultimately to the intended recipient. These transactions were performed to conceal the nature of the funds from law enforcement authorities.

More than a billion dollars moved through the identified cryptocurrency wallet and various financial accounts. Within Figueira’s financial accounts, the majority of the inbound funds were received from cryptocurrency trading platforms. The majority of outbound funds were sent to various businesses and individuals located in the United States and overseas, including high-risk jurisdictions such as Colombia, China, Panamá, and Mexico.

Theophani K. Stamos, First Assistant U.S. Attorney for the Eastern District of Virginia, and Jeffrey L. Tyler, Special Agent in Charge of the FBI Washington Field Office's Criminal Division, made the announcement after sentencing by U.S. District Judge Rossie D. Alston Jr.

Assistant U.S. Attorneys Catherine Rosenberg and Edgardo Rogriguez are prosecuting the case.

Related court documents and information are located on the website of the District Court for the Eastern District of Virginia or on PACER by searching for Case No. 1:26-cr-74.

TULSA, Okla. – Three employees of the U.S. Attorney’s Office for the Northern District of Oklahoma and a detective with the Bartlesville Police Department were among 183 Department of Justice employees recognized by Attorney General Todd Blanche and Executive Office for U.S. Attorneys (EOUSA) Director Francey Hakes at the 2026 Director’s Awards Ceremony held Oct. 28 in Washington, D.C. The annual event honored DOJ employees for outstanding service and achievement and recognized exceptional accomplishments by employees of U.S. Attorneys’ Offices nationwide.

"These awards reflect the extraordinary talent, professionalism, and dedication found throughout our office and community," said U.S. Attorney Christopher J. Nassar. "We are incredibly proud of Thomas, Alicia, Taelyn, and Detective Andrew Bailey for their accomplishments and grateful for their continued service to the Northern District of Oklahoma and the Department of Justice."

Superior Performance in Indian Country

Assistant United States Attorney Alicia Hockenbury and Victim Assistance Specialist Taelyn Langford were recognized with the Director's Award for Superior Performance in Indian Country, alongside the case agent, and Detective Andrew Bailey with Bartlesville Police Department whose critical investigative work was instrumental to the case.

This recognition stems from their outstanding efforts in United States v. Kaleb Smith , in which the defendant was convicted by a jury of Sexual Abuse of a Minor in Indian Country and two counts of Abusive Sexual Contact with a Minor in Indian Country. Court records established that Smith sexually abused two teenage victims, ages 13 and 14. Through the dedication and collaboration of the prosecution team, a sentence of 228 months of imprisonment was secured.

The work of Alicia, Taelyn, and Detective Bailey reflects the highest standards of public service and demonstrates an unwavering commitment to seeking justice for vulnerable victims. Their efforts have made a lasting impact on the lives of those they serve and on the communities they protect.

Excellence of an Appellate Assistant United States Attorney

Thomas Duncombe, Appellate Coordinator for the Northern District of Oklahoma, received the Director's Award for Excellence as an Appellate Assistant United States Attorney. His exceptional legal analysis, advocacy, and steadfast commitment to justice have strengthened the district and advanced the Department of Justice's mission. Thomas was recognized for his written and oral advocacy before the Tenth Circuit Court of Appeals, including his work in United States v. McCarthy . In that case, he successfully argued to the Tenth Circuit to reverse the dismissal of an indictment by demonstrating that the district court had erred in finding that the Controlled Substance Precursor Statutes did not apply to defendants who distributed unwashed poppy seeds while knowing their customers would use them to manufacture opiates. We are grateful for Thomas's leadership and the expertise he brings to every case.

Please join us in congratulating these award recipients on their well-deserved honors. Their achievements exemplify excellence in public service and reflect the strength and commitment of the entire Northern District of Oklahoma team.

Joint Base Andrews marked a historic milestone Nov. 2, with the arrival of the first HH-60W Jolly Green II, bringing a new generation of Air Force rotary-wing capabilities to the nation’s capital for the first time in 60 years.
"Our leaders recognized the need for change and decided to rapidly modernize the equipment that we use to protect our nation,” said Col. Karl W. Seekamp, 316th Wing and installation commander. “...this critical mission deserves the modern capability and safety upgrades that are available today.”
With a larger airframe and bigger fuel capacity, the Jolly Green II can fly faster and farther, extending the operational reach of the Air Force’s response in times of crisis and contingency. It also provides nearly three times the airlift capability of the UH-1N.
The arrival of the Jolly Green II represents a new chapter in the Air Force's rotary-wing history, building on a legacy established by the 1st Helicopter Squadron, which served as the Air Force's only rotary-wing unit in the National Capital Region for six decades.
The aircraft will first be assigned to the 5th Helicopter Squadron, which is charged with training the force and establishing the new fleet, while the 1st HS will fly the UH-1N to provide continuous support of Andrews’ 24/7 no-fail national security mission.
Since 1969, the 1st HS has conducted immediate-response contingency operations in support of critical national security requirements while maintaining a rigorous training schedule to ensure mission readiness. The squadron has flown the UH-1N Huey since 1971, and three of the aircraft that flew during the Vietnam War remain in service today.
That history is an important part of the transition to the Jolly Green II.
“It is important that we honor the legacy of what the Huey has done for safety and operations as a whole,” noted Lt. Col. Jonathan Bonilla, 5th HS commander. “We must remember this while we, as an Air Force, continue to look into the future.”
While the Huey has a storied history of saving lives through its light-lift capabilities, particularly during the Vietnam War, the arrival of the HH-60W represents an investment in modernizing the Andrews’ rotary-wing capabilities and providing a more versatile aircraft to meet evolving operational requirements.
"I think the [HH-60] Whiskey is absolutely the right call," said Capt. Joshua Lemon, 316th Operations Group executive officer and UH-1N instructor pilot, who will be part of the first class of aircrew transitioning to the new aircraft. "It is inherently a joint airframe, meaning that almost any branch or agency in the area can call on us and we can lend a hand, or an aircraft. It makes us part of a bigger team.” 
Although rotary-wing aircraft represent a small but vital part of the Air Force, their maneuverability and ability to operate in areas inaccessible to many fixed-wing aircraft make them essential to a wide range of missions. The arrival of the Jolly Green II ensures JB Andrews' long-term ability to respond to national security requirements across the nation’s capital.
Introducing a new airframe also strengthens the Wing’s readiness for future mission needs and modernizes a crucial fleet of aircraft that supports U.S. senior leaders. Beginning in 2027, designated classes of Airmen from JB Andrews’ helicopter squadrons will receive familiarization training from certified Sikorsky aircrews. Following the course, select Airmen will be qualified to instruct their fellow crewmembers in HH-60W safety and familiarization procedures. As each class graduates, both the 1st and 5th HS will have a growing team of aircrew who can fly both the HH-60W and the UH-1N, enabling 24/7 continuous support.
As the Jolly Green II takes its place on the JB Andrews flightline, it carries forward a mission shaped by decades of service. The Huey's legacy remains an enduring part of that history, while the arrival of the HH-60W ensures the installation is equipped to meet the demands of the future.
title: First HH-60W arrives at JB Andrews, marking new era for Air Force rotary-wing operations

Release Number 9320-26
CFTC Secures Court Order Directing Texas Man and His Company to Pay Over $13 Million in Commodities Fraud
November 03, 2026
WASHINGTON — The Commodity Futures Trading Commission today announced the U.S. District Court for the Northern District of Texas entered a default judgment against defendants Walter Dunning Larrick III and Cambridge Financial Advisors LLC for their participation in a commodities fraud scheme.
In entering the default judgment, the court found the defendants fraudulently solicited and misappropriated more than $3 million from participants.
The court found the defendants falsely represented they would use participant funds to trade futures and options, including those involving natural gas, oil, and gold; made material misrepresentations and omissions about the profitability of commodity trading with them; and issued false account statements to conceal their misconduct.
The court further found the defendants misappropriated participant funds by making payments to existing participants in a manner akin to a Ponzi scheme, paying Larrick’s personal expenses, and sending funds to offshore accounts in Costa Rica.
The court ordered the defendants to pay a $9,767,625 civil monetary penalty and $3,255,875 in restitution. It also permanently enjoined them from further violations of the Commodity Exchange Act and Commission regulations, as charged, and imposed permanent trading and registration bans.
The default judgment resolves all claims in the CFTC’s 2023 complaint. [See CFTC Press Release No. 8768-23.]

ICE HSI New Jersey arrests Jamaican national accused of voting illegally over 22-year span
WASHINGTON — ICE’s Homeland Security Investigations New Jersey arrested Antonio Mitchell Oct. 28 for illegally voting in a range of elections between 2000 and 2022. Mitchell, a 54-year-old lawful permanent resident from Jamaica, has arrests for burglary, resisting arrest, and possession of marijuana for sale. These charges were ultimately dropped.
“Voting in American elections is a right reserved for eligible voters,” said ICE Assistant Director of Public Affairs Micah Bock. “Those who knowingly violate federal election laws should understand that their actions carry serious consequences. ICE cannot ignore suspected federal crimes simply because they involve elections. The law applies to everyone, and we intend to enforce it.”
According to investigators, Mitchell registered to vote and participated in multiple federal primary and general elections over a 22-year span, despite being ineligible because he was not a U.S. citizen.
In January 2025, Mitchell submitted a naturalization application in which he allegedly falsely stated he had never registered to vote or voted in a federal, state or local election. Those statements became part of a joint investigation involving HSI, the FBI and U.S. Citizenship and Immigration Services.
Federal law generally prohibits noncitizens, including lawful permanent residents, from voting in elections for federal office. Knowingly making materially false statements during the naturalization process carries criminal penalties.
title: ICE HSI New Jersey arrests Jamaican national accused of voting illegally over 22-year span

BIRMINGHAM, Ala. – A convicted felon has been sentenced for illegal possession of multiple firearms, announced U.S. Attorney Phillip W. Williams Jr.

U.S. District Court Judge Anna M. Manasco sentenced Timothy Shane Postell, 40, of Bessemer, Alabama, to 130 months in prison. Postell pleaded guilty to being a felon in possession of a firearm in two separate and unrelated cases.

According to the plea agreements, Postell illegally possessed firearms on two separate occasions.

On April 16, 2022, an officer with the Leeds Police Department responded to a call at a retail store in Leeds. The officer arrived on the scene and found a female and Postell on a couch, and both appeared to be under the influence of narcotics. They were arrested for public intoxication. The officer searched Postell and recovered a stolen pair of tennis shoes, narcotics, and a loaded SCCY 9mm pistol.

On February 7, 2026, an officer with the Hueytown Police Department initiated a traffic stop on a vehicle driven by Postell. As the officer approached the vehicle, Postell fled the scene recklessly—speeding and passing vehicles with oncoming traffic and in no-passing zones. The pursuit continued until Postell stopped at the end of a dirt road. Postell exited the vehicle and ran. An officer deployed his taser with no effect but eventually got close enough to tackle Postell and handcuff him. The officer searched Postell and recovered a loaded Canik 9mm pistol from one of Postell’s inside jacket pockets and a loaded Glock 10mm pistol from the other inside jacket pocket. During a search of Postell’s vehicle, officers recovered a loaded Marlin .22 rifle, body armor plates, methamphetamine, and drug paraphernalia.

“Keeping firearms out of the hands of convicted felons is critical in protecting our communities,” said U.S. Attorney Williams. “This defendant repeatedly demonstrated disregard for the law. This 130-month sentence sends a clear message that illegal firearm possession by repeat offenders will have serious consequences. We are grateful to our law enforcement partners for their dedication and continued efforts to keep our communities safe.”

“ATF prioritizes public safety and is committed to bringing individuals who unlawfully possess firearms to justice” said ATF Special Agent in Charge James VanVliet. “Mr. Postell, a four-time convicted felon, showed a pattern of criminal behavior in this case, illegally possessing firearms in multiple incidents. ATF will continue to work with our state and local law enforcement partners to make our communities safe by pursuing, apprehending, and prosecuting such individuals who demonstrate a propensity for lawlessness and recklessness.”

Postell is prohibited from possessing firearms because of his four prior felony convictions that span from 2007 to 2021. Postell was convicted in the Superior Court of Paulding County, Georgia in February 2007, of Robbery by Intimidation, Theft by Taking, and Aggravated Assault and in September 2013, of Possession of Cocaine; in the Circuit Court of Jefferson County, Alabama in May 2014 for Robbery, Second Degree; and in the District Court of Shelby County, Alabama in February 2021, of Burglary, Third Degree.

The ATF investigated the case along with the Leeds Police Department and Hueytown Police Department. Assistant United States Attorney Darius C. Greene prosecuted the case.
title: Four-Time Convicted Felon Sentenced to More than 10 Years in Prison for Illegal Possession of Multiple Firearms

WASHINGTON – The United States Attorney for the District of Columbia announced today that Strand Book Store, Inc. has agreed to pay $1,482,560 because the New York City bookstore violated the False Claims Act by improperly applying for and receiving a second draw loan under the Paycheck Protection Program (PPP) for which it was not eligible. Strand was ineligible because Senator Ron Wyden’s wife was the owner.

“The Paycheck Protection Program was created to save American jobs, not to enrich those who aren’t eligible for taxpayer-funded relief, especially the wife of a U.S. Senator,” said U.S. Attorney Pirro. “Strand Book Store, owned by Nancy Bass Wyden, wife of U.S. Senator Ron Wyden, received $932,350 in second draw PPP funds despite a federal law barring businesses controlled by a member of Congress or their spouse from receiving those loans. Our Fraud and Asset Recovery Division will expose this abuse, pursue those who exploit taxpayer dollars, and hold them accountable. No one gets a pass when it comes to defrauding the American taxpayer.”

“The Paycheck Protection Program was created to save American jobs, not to enrich those who aren’t eligible for taxpayer-funded relief, especially the wife of a U.S. Senator,” said U.S. Attorney Pirro. “Strand Book Store, owned by Nancy Bass Wyden, wife of U.S. Senator Ron Wyden, received $932,350 in second draw PPP funds despite a federal law barring businesses controlled by a member of Congress or their spouse from receiving those loans. Our Fraud and Asset Recovery Division will expose this abuse, pursue those who exploit taxpayer dollars, and hold them accountable. No one gets a pass when it comes to defrauding the American taxpayer.”

When Congress enacted the Coronavirus, Aid, Relief, and Economic Security (CARES) Act in March 2020, it authorized forgivable PPP loans to eligible small businesses and nonprofit organizations for job retention and certain other expenses. The PPP loan program was administered by the Small Business Administration. In the Economic Aid to Hard-Hit Small Businesses, Nonprofits, and Venues Act enacted in December 2020, Congress provided additional funding for PPP loans and allowed eligible entities to apply for a “second draw” of PPP funding. The Economic Aid Act included a prohibition against businesses obtaining second draw PPP funds if a member of Congress or their spouse directly or indirectly held a controlling interest in the PPP loan applicant.

In February 2021, Strand applied for a second draw PPP loan in the amount of $932,350. At the time, the controlling owner of Strand was Nancy Bass Wyden, the wife of U.S. Senator Ron Wyden. On behalf of Strand, Ms. Wyden made a number of certifications as part of the loan application, including that the spouse of a Member of Congress does not directly or indirectly hold a controlling interest in the applicant. Ms. Wyden’s certification was knowingly and materially false and Strand was not eligible for the second draw loan it received.

The settlement resolves claims brought under the qui tam or whistleblower provisions of the False Claims Act. Under these provisions, a private party can file an action on behalf of the United States and receive a portion of the recovery. The qui tam complaint was filed by a corporate Relator Blockquote Inc. and is captioned U.S. ex rel. Blockquote Inc. v. Strand Book Store, Inc., Civ. No. 25-3609 (D.D.C.) . Blockquote Inc. will receive a total share of approximately $148,256 in connection with the settlement.

The civil settlement resulted from an investigation by Assistant United States Attorney Sean M. Tepe with the support of attorney Christopher J. McClintock of SBA’s Office of the General Counsel. This is the second recovery on behalf of the United States since U.S. Attorney Pirro announced the creation of the Fraud and Asset Recovery Division, headed by Assistant U.S. Attorney Dan Schiffer.

Tips and complaint regarding potential fraud affecting COVID-19 government relief programs can be reported by calling the Department of Justice’s National Center for Disaster Fraud (NCDF) Hotline at (866) 720-5721 or by submitting a NCDF Web Complaint form at https://www.justice.gov/disaster-fraud/ncdf-disaster-complaint-form .

On April 7, the Department of Justice announced the creation of the National Fraud Enforcement Division. The Fraud Division is laser-focused on investigating and prosecuting those who commit fraud against the American people. The Department’s work to combat fraud supports President Trump’s Task Force to Eliminate Fraud, a whole-of-government effort chaired by Vice President J.D. Vance to eliminate fraud, waste, and abuse within Federal benefit programs.

The claims resolved by the civil settlement are allegations only, and there has been no determination of liability.

WASHINGTON – One of the Department of Justice’s (DOJ) most important missions is ensuring election integrity, supporting free and fair elections, and protecting the right to vote for U.S. citizens across the United States. The DOJ has sent election monitors in support of this mission since the enactment of the Voting Rights Act in 1965 across all Administrations.

Today, the DOJ will further this mission by engaging in its largest monitoring effort in history—with approximately 1,000 election monitors and observers deployed, and, for the first time, in all 50 states. The effort is coordinated by the Civil Rights Division. Monitors will include personnel from the Division, other DOJ divisions/components, U.S. Attorney’s Offices and federal observers from the Office of Personnel Management. Throughout Election Day, Division personnel will maintain contact with state and local election officials.

“Election integrity has been one of the top priorities for this Administration and this Division,” said Assistant Attorney General Harmeet K. Dhillon of the Civil Rights Division at the Department of Justice. “I am very proud we are deploying the largest monitoring effort in DOJ history, and pursuing transparency for elections in an assertive and nondiscriminatory manner.”

Election monitors will be checking for compliance with the federal voting rights statutes that fall within the jurisdiction of the Division. The Division’s Voting Section enforces the civil provisions of federal statutes that protect the right to vote, including the Voting Rights Act, National Voter Registration Act, Help America Vote Act, Uniformed and Overseas Citizens Absentee Voting Act, and Civil Rights Acts.

The Division’s Disability Rights Section enforces the Americans with Disabilities Act (ADA) to ensure that persons with disabilities have a full and equal opportunity to vote. The Division’s Criminal Section enforces federal criminal statutes that prohibit voter intimidation and voter suppression based on race, color, national origin, or religion.

Throughout the day and week, Division personnel will be available to receive questions and complaints from the public related to federal voting rights laws. If you have a question or complaint, please call our election issues hotline at 1-800-253-3931, email us at VEM@usdoj.gov , or submit a complaint through our website at www.civilrights.justice.gov/report .

Individuals with questions or complaints related to the ADA may call the Division’s toll-free ADA information hotline at 1-800-514-0301 or 1-833-610-1264 (TTY) or submit a complaint through our ADA website at www.ada.gov .

Complaints related to any disruptions at a polling place should always be reported to local election officials (including officials based in the polling place). Complaints related to violence, threats of violence or intimidation at a polling place should be reported immediately to local police authorities by calling 911. These complaints should also be reported to the department after local authorities have been contacted.

To learn more about what the DOJ and the Civil Rights Division has done historically to protect the vote and ensure free and fair elections, go to www.civilrights.justice.gov/electionintegrity .

BOSTON – A Mexican national unlawfully residing in Jamaica Plain, Mass. pleaded guilty to unlawfully reentering the United States after deportation.

Carlos Altunar-Rueda, 33, pleaded guilty to a one count indictment. U.S. District Court Leo T. Sorokin scheduled sentencing for Jan. 27, 2027. Altunar-Rueda was indicted by a federal grand jury in June 2026. In January 2026, he was charged by criminal complaint with the same offense.

Altunar-Rueda is a citizen of Mexico who was deported from the United States in 2013 and again in 2019. In May 2018 , he was convicted in federal court in Massachusetts for unlawful reentry of a deported alien. In November 2015, he was convicted in New York state court for sexual abuse in the 3rd degree, sexual abuse in the 2nd degree and forcible touching. The charge of unlawful reentry of a deported alien provides for a sentence of up to 10 years in prison, three years of supervised release and a fine of up to $250,000. The defendant is subject to deportation upon completion of any sentence imposed. Sentences are imposed by a federal district court judge based upon the U.S. Sentencing Guidelines and statutes which govern the determination of a sentence in a criminal case.

United States Attorney Leah B. Foley and David T. Wesling, Acting Field Office Director of U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement’s Enforcement and Removal Operations in Boston made the announcement. Assistant U.S. Attorney Suzanne Sullivan Jacobus of the Major Crimes Unit is prosecuting the case.
title: Illegal Alien from Mexico Pleads Guilty to Illegal Reentry

Representative Min and Senator Welch Demand Answers from Former Trump Attorney Alina Habba-Mildon on Influence over President’s Pardon of Corrupt Venezuelan Banker Julio Herrera Velutini
Washington, DC. — U.S. Representative Dave Min (D-CA-47), Member of the House Committee on Oversight and Government Reform and Chair of the Congressional Progressive Caucus’ Anti-Corruption Task Force and U.S. Senator Peter Welch (D-Vt.), Ranking Member of the Senate Judiciary Subcommittee on the Constitution, are demanding answers from former Senior Adviser to the Attorney General Alina Mildon on her reported role in President Trump’s decision to grant Julio Herrera Velutini—who pleaded guilty to violating U.S. campaign finance laws—a full presidential pardon. The letters come as President Trump criticized his former attorney’s $50 million agreement with Mr. Herrera as “totally obnoxious and outrageous,” and “not acceptable.”
In their letters, the lawmakers express concern that the timing of Ms. Habba-Mildon’s hiring and Mr. Herrera’s daughter’s contribution to MAGA Inc. raise questions about whether improper considerations, including quid pro quo or “pay-to-play” dynamics, may have affected President Trump’s decision to pardon him. These letters are part of a broader bicameral investigation led by Representative Min and Senator Welch into potential corruption surrounding President Trump’s decisions to grant presidential pardons.
The lawmakers write: “Article II, Section 2, Clause 1 of the U.S. Constitution authorizes the President to ‘grant Reprieves and Pardons for Offenses against the United States, except in Cases of Impeachment.’ The U.S. Supreme Court has characterized executive clemency as ‘an act of grace’ exercised for the ‘public welfare.’ President Trump’s use of this authority appears to deviate from this traditional purpose. Congress has a compelling interest in ensuring that the constitutional pardon power is exercised with fairness and transparency. Given these circumstances, we are seeking additional information to better understand the extent to which influence and access may have overridden the standard pardon review process.”
In August 2022, Mr. Herrera was criminally charged with providing $300,000 to a super political action committee (PAC) in violation of a campaign finance law barring contributions or donations by foreign nationals to U.S. federal, state, or local elections. Mr. Herrera financially supported the reelection campaign of Puerto Rico’s governor in exchange for her pledge to remove a top banking regulator who had scrutinized one of Mr. Herrera’s banks.
According to public reporting, Ms. Mildon entered into an employment agreement with Mr. Herrera’s family in late 2025, while she was serving as an adviser at the Justice Department. She also previously served as President Trump’s personal lawyer and as the Acting U.S. Attorney for New Jersey. In the hiring contract, Mr. Velutini’s family agreed to pay her $50 million over four years to be general counsel at Concord Partners, a company set up by Mr. Velutini’s daughter days before she signed the contract. Ms. Mildon finalized the deal with Concord Partners while she was still serving at the Justice Department.
Ms. Mildon then began working for Concord Partners on January 1, 2026, while serving as a senior adviser to then-Attorney General Pam Bondi, overseeing U.S. attorneys. Two weeks later, Mr. Herrera received a pardon on January 15, 2026. Since President Trump’s election in November 2024, his 27-year-old daughter, a self-employed financial consultant, also donated $3.5 million to MAGA Inc., a Trump-supporting super PAC.
Read and download the lawmakers’ full letters to Alina Habba-Mildon and Julio Herrera Velutini.
In May, Senator Welch and Rep. Min sent letters to 17 individuals who received pardons or commutations under circumstances that warrant further congressional scrutiny, including several individuals connected to major fraud schemes, financial crimes, and high-profile political or financial relationships tied to President Trump and his associates. The earlier letters sought information regarding the clemency process, including whether financial contributions, lobbyists, intermediaries, or personal connections played a role in securing presidential clemency.
Among the individuals who received letters are convicted fraudsters, political fundraisers, corporate executives, and wealthy donors, such as Changpeng Zhao, whose cases have generated public reporting suggesting unusual access to Trump’s network of political allies and associates, direct lobbying efforts, large political donations, or other concerning connections surrounding their clemency requests.
The lawmakers continued their investigation in June, sending four additional letters to the Department of Justice’s Office of the Pardon Attorney, the White House Office of Records Management, the White House Pardon Czar, and the United States Secret Service. In October, the lawmakers initiated a probe into the influence of cabinet members, U.S. Health and Human Services (HHS) Secretary Robert F. Kennedy, Jr., and Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) Administrator Lee Zeldin, in Trump’s decision to pardon convicted felons.

title: Representative Min and Senator Welch Demand Answers from Former Trump Attorney Alina Habba-Mildon on Influence over President’s Pardon of Corrupt Venezuelan Banker Julio Herrera Velutini

Media Note

Bureau of Arms Control and Nonproliferation

November 3, 2026

On October 27–29, 2026 in Split, Croatia, the United States and the Republic of Croatia co-hosted a Southeast Europe Proliferation Security Initiative (PSI) engagement. This regional event is a continuation of the strong regional security partnership and marks the fifth time Croatia has hosted a PSI activity. The engagement and exercise convened more than 70 participants from 22 countries and included civilian, law enforcement, and military leaders from Austria, Bosnia and Herzegovina, Bulgaria, Croatia, Czechia, Estonia, France, Germany, Greece, Hungary, Italy, Kosovo, Moldova, Montenegro, North Macedonia, Poland, Romania, Slovakia, Slovenia, Switzerland, Türkiye, the United Kingdom, and the United States.

Participants evaluated current proliferation challenges, techniques used to evade sanctions, other relevant control mechanisms, and trends in the Adriatic and Southeast Europe. Participants also heard from experts on proliferation finance and explored the legal frameworks needed to interdict proliferation-related cargo. Specific attention was given to post-interdiction considerations, including avenues to dispose of proliferation-sensitive cargo. Croatia presented a case study demonstrating how PSI partners can prevent transfers of dual-use goods and sensitive technologies to countries of proliferation concern.

Delegates also participated in a tabletop exercise that required them to identify the authorities and agreements available to prevent a multifaceted proliferation-related transfer and coordinate their actions within their own governments and with regional partners. Participants also observed a live interdiction exercise at the Port of Split that featured Croatian authorities boarding and detaining a vessel and disposing of its illicit cargo.

The PSI Southeast Europe Engagement series advances regional security by building the capabilities that partners need to interdict proliferation-related transfers, strengthening export control and sanctions implementation, and reinforcing states’ ability to meet their obligations under UN Security Council Resolution 1540.

Countries join the PSI by endorsing the PSI Statement of Interdiction Principles, making a political commitment to disrupt proliferation-related transfers, consistent with national legal authorities and relevant international frameworks. To date, 116 states have endorsed these Principles.

Muncy McAllister, III, age 39, of Denham Springs, Louisiana, pleaded guilty to three counts of wire fraud before U.S. District Judge Brian A. Jackson in connection with his scheme to obtain funds from a federal pandemic assistance program by submitting false and fraudulent applications.

According to admissions made as part of his guilty plea, McAllister submitted two fraudulent EIDL applications in August of 2020, one in his own name and one in the name of Famtight. Both applications falsely claimed significant business revenue, multiple employees and that he had no recent felony convictions. Based on these misrepresentations, McAllister attempted to get over $177,000 in EIDL loans.

“This office will continue to safeguard federal relief programs intended to support legitimate small businesses,” U.S. Attorney Wall said. “Individuals who defraud these programs, especially during a national emergency, will be held accountable.”

The case was investigated and prosecuted by the U.S. Attorney’s Office for the Middle District of Louisiana. Assistant U.S. Attorney Jessica M.P. Thornhill, who also serves a Deputy Criminal Chief, led the prosecution.

On April 7, the Department of Justice announced the creation of the National Fraud Enforcement Division (“Fraud Division”). The Fraud Division is laser-focused on investigating and prosecuting those who commit fraud against the American people. The Department’s work to combat fraud supports President Trump’s Task Force to Eliminate Fraud, a whole-of-government effort chaired by Vice President J.D. Vance to eliminate fraud, waste, and abuse within Federal benefit programs.

BOSTON – A Rockland, Mass. man has been charged with a second count of drug distribution which allegedly resulted in the death of a victim in Slippery Rock, Penn. in October 2025.

Jaden Zion Andre, 23, has been charged in a superseding indictment with a second count of drug distribution resulting in death. Andre was previously indicted in August 2026 with eight counts of drug distribution, including one count of drug distribution that resulted in the death of a victim in Las Vegas, Nev., in April 2025.

According to the charging documents, Andre operated a Telegram channel called “MontanaSnacksLLC” and a Proton Mail account called “SnackSeason,” which he used to communicate with his drug customers. As part of his operation, Andre allegedly concealed his synthetic opioids in snack bags, which he then distributed through the United States mail to his customers across the country.

On Oct. 3, 2025, a package allegedly shipped through “SnackSeason” was delivered to a woman in Pennsylvania who had requested a narcotics sample. The package had been mailed on Oct. 1, 2025, at approximately 4:12 p.m. from a post office in Lowell, Mass. The woman was found dead three days later. A residual substance recovered from the crime scene tested positive for N-propionitrile chlorphine (Cychlorphine), an analogue of the schedule I controlled substance brorphine. A review of the woman’s cell phone allegedly revealed messages between her account and SnackSeason, which was believed to be operated by Andre:

According to the charging documents, Andre had previously mailed a package containing Cychlorphine to an officer acting in an undercover capacity on Aug. 2, 2025, at approximately 1:01 p.m., from a post office in Worcester, Mass.

It is alleged that Andre’s drug trafficking operation continued through May 2026, with additional packages from MontanaSnacksLLC or SnackSeason connected to overdose deaths in Florida and Georgia. Those deaths remain under investigation.

The charge of distribution of controlled substances resulting in death provides for a sentence of no less than 20 years and up to life in prison, at least three years of supervised release and a fine of up to $1 million. Sentences are imposed by a federal district court judge based upon the U.S. Sentencing Guidelines and statutes which govern the determination of a sentence in a criminal case.

United States Attorney Leah B. Foley; Jeffrey Grimming, Acting Special Agent in Charge of Homeland Security Investigations; Jarod A. Forget, Special Agent in Charge of the Drug Enforcement Administration, New England Field Division; and Justin Page, Acting Inspector in Charge of the U.S. Postal Inspection Service’s Boston Division made the announcement today. Valuable assistance was provided by the Las Vegas Metropolitan Police Department Overdose Response Team; United States Postal Inspection Service, Las Vegas and Pittsburgh Field Offices; Federal Bureau of Investigation, Las Vegas Division; Hillsborough County Sheriff’s Office (Florida); DEA Pittsburgh District Office; Pennsylvania State Police; Butler City Police Department (Pennsylvania); and the Massachusetts State Police. Special Assistant United States Attorney Michael E. Robinson of the Narcotics & Money Laundering Unit is prosecuting the case.

This case is part of the Homeland Security Task Force (HSTF) initiative established by Executive Order 14159, Protecting the American People Against Invasion. The HSTF is a whole-of-government partnership dedicated to eliminating criminal cartels, foreign gangs, transnational criminal organizations, and human smuggling and trafficking rings operating in the United States and abroad. Through historic interagency collaboration, the HSTF directs the full might of United States law enforcement towards identifying, investigating, and prosecuting the full spectrum of crimes committed by these organizations, which have long fueled violence and instability within our borders. In performing this work, the HSTF places special emphasis on investigating and prosecuting those engaged in child trafficking or other crimes involving children. The HSTF further utilizes all available tools to prosecute and remove the most violent criminal aliens from the United States. HSTF Boston is comprised of agents and officers from HSI, FBI, DEA, ATF, USMS, IRS-CI, USPIS, DOL-OIG, DSS and CBP as well as several state and local law enforcement agencies, with the prosecution being led by the United States Attorney’s Office for the District of Massachusetts.

The details contained in the charging document are allegations. The defendant is presumed to be innocent unless and until proven guilty beyond a reasonable doubt in the court of law.
title: Massachusetts Man Charged with Distributing Synthetic Opioids that Resulted in Second Death

WICHITA, KAN. – A federal grand jury in Wichita returned an indictment today charging a Kansas postal worker with stealing thousands of pieces of mail, including hundreds of political mailings that were all related to Republican Party candidates.

According to court documents, Kelly R. Cram, 59, of Baxter Springs, was indicted on one count of unlawful secretion, destruction, and delay of mail.

Beginning in October 2026, Cram is accused of stealing 4,404 pieces of mail that were intended to be delivered to customers in and around Pittsburg, Kansas. Among the mail items she allegedly stole and placed in her garage, were nearly 400 political mailers solely related to Republican candidates or Republican Partly affiliated political action committees. Agents found no mailers related to candidates of any other political party at Cram’s residence.

The U.S. Postal Service – Office of Inspector General (USPS-OIG) is investigating the case.

text:
ARLINGTON, Va. – For U.S. Army Sgt. 1st Class Amber Peck, finding reliable childcare became one of the greatest challenges of serving in the Wisconsin Army National Guard. As a co-parent in a dual-military family, overlapping drill weekends often meant scrambling to find childcare for her daughter, sometimes relying on relatives or even flying a family member in from Puerto Rico.
“I felt like I was constantly pressuring my family for help, not receiving it and feeling like I'd rather just not be in the military because it was such a consistent burden that I simply had no fix for,” Peck said.
She added that the recurring challenge eventually made her question whether she could continue her military career.
For Soldiers facing similar challenges, the Army National Guard’s Weekend Drill Childcare program provides eligible Soldiers with reliable, no-cost childcare during scheduled drill weekends. The program is expanding from a 20-state pilot to all 50 states, three territories and the District of Columbia by Dec. 31, according to U.S. Army Col. Danielle MacDonnell, chief of the human resources directorate at the National Guard Bureau, which supports approximately 330,000 Soldiers.
She said the childcare program gives Soldiers and families more flexibility by letting them seek care near their home or drill location.
“Free childcare for our traditional drilling Guardsmen relieved a large amount of stress for families when planning to attend drill and managing family responsibilities,” MacDonnell said. “By relieving the burden of childcare, Soldiers are more able to focus during drill weekends and perform at higher levels.”
Feedback from the pilot program indicated that access to childcare can reduce family stress, remove a potential barrier to drill attendance and support readiness and retention efforts, MacDonnell said.
For Peck, coordinating traditional childcare arrangements for weekend drills was often difficult. Family members had their own weekend commitments, and most childcare facilities operated during the workweek. At one point, Peck turned to an online babysitting service but remained uneasy about leaving her daughter with someone she had only recently met.
When Wisconsin participated in the pilot program, Peck said the program offered something more important than financial savings: consistency and peace of mind.
“It was the consistent, close, reliable care that made a huge difference,” Peck said. “Having someone who I knew would have their door open for my daughter one weekend every month was huge.”
The provider was located within a few miles of Peck’s armory, making childcare more convenient during lengthy drill days.
“My daughter received care from the program for about eight months, and it ended up being a home she didn’t want to leave at the end of the day,” Peck said. “That made me feel so grateful and at ease.”
In Texas, Army National Guard leaders received information about the expansion Sept. 28 through a personnel update, according to Shandra Sponsler, personnel services branch chief for the Texas Army National Guard.
Sponsler said the Texas Army National Guard plans to share information about the program through unit chains of command, digital flyers, email and text alerts, social media, child and youth services personnel and family-readiness networks.
“This program has the capability to assist in alleviating the stress of finding childcare when a spouse or domestic partner must work and the social-support network is lacking or nonexistent,” Sponsler said.
Sponsler said the program may be especially important for dual-military couples, who can face competing drill schedules and childcare requirements.
“Reliable childcare during drill weekends enables Soldiers to focus on mission-critical tasks with peace of mind that their children are well cared for,” Sponsler said.
For MacDonnell, the program also has a personal connection.
“At one point, I was a single parent myself,” MacDonnell said. “Being able to provide this benefit to Soldiers removes one less stress in their lives and enables them to focus on what they need to do for themselves, as well as for the organization.”
For Peck, dependable childcare removed a burden that once threatened her willingness to keep serving.
“Having that reliable childcare completely put my mind at ease for drill weekends and 100% allowed me to focus on what I needed to for the military,” Peck said.
Asked how she would describe the program’s value to Army National Guard leadership, Peck offered a one-word answer.
“Invaluable.”
Peck’s experience reflects how reliable childcare can help remove a practical barrier to service for Guard families.
“We recruit Soldiers, but we retain families, because behind every Soldier is a family serving alongside them,” said Senior Enlisted Advisor John Raines, SEA to the chief of the National Guard Bureau. “By ensuring no Soldier has to choose between their job and childcare on drill weekends, this initiative helps soften a barrier to service and strengthens readiness across the force.”
title: Army National Guard expands Weekend Drill Child Care Program

ABERDEEN PROVING GROUND, Md.– “Proactive Analysis: Delivering a Decision Advantage” was the theme of the U.S. Army Operations Research Symposium, known as AORS, from Sep. 14-16. Participants were able to attend in person and virtually via MS Teams.
The U.S. Army Transformation Decision Analysis Center, known as TDAC, hosted this year’s multi-day event, which included 361 registered in person and virtual attendees. With over 82 presentations, attendees represented more than 34 organizations and 12 working groups.
TDAC Director, Larry Larimer, kicked the event off with a welcome message, sharing, “We as operations research and systems analysts (ORSAs) are to look over the horizon. We need to look at what our analysis is telling us, what the data is telling us, and be prepared to use that existing data we generated to answer questions”.
The annual event provides members of the Army’s analytic community, including U.S. government employees, contractors and approved foreign personnel from partner nations such as the United Kingdom, Republic of Korea and Germany, an opportunity to share professional knowledge gained from ongoing and completed analysis. AORS allows analysts to meet with colleagues, exchange experiences and insights appropriate for general and international audiences, and participate in constructive dialogue designed to challenge, broaden and expand the perspective of the analytical community.
This year, AORS also featured an organizational showcase hosted by operations research/systems analysis (ORSA) professionals. The showcase brought together Army officers (Functional Area 49) with data and quantitative analysis expertise and Civilian members of the Analysis, Modeling and Simulation Career Program (CP 36) where they provided organizational and technological overviews, highlighted career advancement opportunities and afforded participants an additional venue for networking.
Lt. Gen. Michael “Mac” McCurry, commanding general, U.S. Army Futures and Autonomous Systems Command served as keynote speaker by providing remarks remotely from the Pentagon.
McCurry’s keynote remarks focused on the Army’s shift from organizational restructuring to improving the processes that support faster, more effective decision-making as it modernizes for future warfare. He emphasized the growing role of analysts in helping commanders make sense of increasingly larger volumes of battlefield data, using artificial intelligence effectively and anticipating senior leaders’ decision needs. He said the Army must combine technology, data, rigorous analysis and human judgment to accelerate decisions while ensuring increased speed does not come at the expense of sound decision-making.
McCurry said, “Data alone can inundate and slow down a commander. Data with the right analysis is a game changer.” He continued to emphasize, “As you do your rigorous analysis, we need you to anticipate senior leaders' needs so that we're one step ahead to make those decisions faster.”
During the first day of AORS, the ORSA Hall of Fame induction and Army Analysis Awards ceremonies were held. The ORSA Hall of Fame honors those individuals who have contributed significantly to ORSA over a sustained period, have significantly influenced ORSA through doctrinal or technical accomplishment and innovative development, and have demonstrated outstanding personal leadership and noteworthy achievements that inspired others in operations research.
This year’s inductees were John Thomas and Allan Resnick.
During a nearly 40-year career, Thomas advanced Army analysis and modeling and simulation by developing innovative methodologies and pioneering capabilities in directed energy, target acquisition, anti-armor systems and Soldier-in-the-loop simulation. His work influenced major Army acquisition and programming decisions, helped develop and validate OneSAF, strengthened Army modeling and simulation capabilities, and earned recognition for his technical expertise and service to soldiers and civilians.
Resnick, throughout his career, helped shape Army analysis and modernization by developing influential analytical concepts and models addressing artillery survivability, ammunition resupply and future force structure. He directed major cost and operational effectiveness analyses for systems including Patriot PAC-III, ATACMS and AFATDS, helping ensure significant acquisition decisions were supported by objective analysis. Resnick also developed the Capabilities Needs Analysis, establishing an enduring Army framework for identifying and assessing mission requirements.
After the hall of fame inductees were completed, additional awards recipients were recognized:

Day one also featured a panel discussion with senior Army leaders, including Chris Barrett, executive director of the Army Evaluation Center; John Helms, technical director of the Center for Army Analysis; Cody Beck, deputy director of TDAC; and Col. Sean Madden, chief data science officer for U.S. Army Western Hemisphere Command.
This panel’s discussion focused on current operational decision cycles and rapid technological disruption that demands a decisive shift from traditional, protracted analysis toward proactive, agile analytic support. In this session, senior leaders examined the strategic imperatives facing the analytic community. Panelists addressed balancing analytic speed with rigor, ensuring standardized data accessibility in theater, and overcoming workforce deficits stemming from recent hiring constraints and personnel shaping initiatives.
The discussion also explored modern mentorship models required to accelerate junior analyst readiness, strategies to dismantle joint and allied data silos, and practical approaches to communicating uncertainty so operational commanders can act on complex analysis with complete confidence.

BOWLING GREEN, KY – A Barren County, Kentucky, man was sentenced on October 26, 2026, to 20 years in prison for methamphetamine trafficking.

U.S. Attorney Kyle G. Bumgarner of the Western District of Kentucky, Special Agent in Charge Olivia Olson of the FBI Louisville Field Office, and Director Ron Lafferty of the Barren River Drug Task Force made the announcement.

Shane Stuart Wheat, 35, was sentenced to 20 years in federal prison, followed by 10 years of supervised release, for trafficking in over 159.08 grams of methamphetamine. Notably, Wheat had previously been convicted of drug trafficking five times, with three of those offenses subjecting him to increased penalties. Specifically:

On December 9, 2021, Wheat was convicted of trafficking in a controlled substance, first degree, second or greater offense, involving more than 2 grams of methamphetamine.

On September 25, 2017, Wheat was convicted of trafficking in a controlled substance, first degree, second or greater offense, involving more than 2 grams of methamphetamine.

On September 25, 2017, Wheat was convicted of trafficking in a controlled substance, first degree, second or greater offense, involving more than 2 grams of methamphetamine.

Wheat’s criminal history made him a “career offender” under the federal sentencing guidelines.

United States Attorney Kyle Bumgarner stated, “Twenty years in prison is a significant sentence which reflects the fact that Wheat was simply determined to remain a drug dealer for his entire life. It is almost incomprehensible that Wheat had previously been convicted of drug trafficking five times yet continued to peddle drugs. His drug trafficking career is over for two decades thanks to the important work of the Barren River Drug Task Force and the FBI.”

“The Homeland Security Task Force is working tirelessly alongside our partners to target career criminals and drug trafficking organizations who threaten the safety and security of our neighborhoods, said FBI Special Agent in Charge Olivia Olson. “The FBI will continue to use every available resource to pursue justice for those who think they can operate outside of the law.”

Barren River Drug Task Force Director Ron Lafferty stated, “The Barren River Drug Task Force appreciates the combined efforts by working with the FBI to help fight the drug problem in Barren County."

There is no parole in the federal system.

This case was investigated by the FBI Bowling Green Resident Agency and the Barren River Drug Task Force.

Assistant U.S. Attorney Mark J. Yurchisin II of the U.S. Attorney’s Bowling Green Branch Office prosecuted the case.

This prosecution is part of the Homeland Security Task Force (HSTF) initiative established by Executive Order 14159, Protecting the American People Against Invasion. The HSTF is a whole-of-government partnership dedicated to eliminating criminal cartels, foreign gangs, transnational criminal organizations, and human smuggling and trafficking rings operating in the United States and abroad. Through historic interagency collaboration, the HSTF directs the full might of United States law enforcement towards identifying, investigating, and prosecuting the full spectrum of crimes committed by these organizations, which have long fueled violence and instability within our borders. In performing this work, the HSTF places special emphasis on investigating and prosecuting those engaged in child trafficking or other crimes involving children. The HSTF further utilizes all available tools to prosecute and remove the most violent criminal aliens from the United States. HSTF Louisville comprises agents and officers from FBI, HSI, DEA, ATF, and IRS, with the prosecution being led by the United States Attorney’s Office for the Western District of Kentucky.

BOSTON – Two men have been indicted by a federal grand jury in Boston for allegedly conspiring to distribute cocaine.

Eduardo Gomez-Santana, 50, of Providence, R.I. and Isaac Marrero, 33, of Middleboro, Mass. were indicted on one count each of conspiracy to distribute 500 grams or more of cocaine and distribution of 500 grams or more of cocaine. Both defendants were arrested and charged in September 2026. Gomez-Santana is currently detained pending trial and Marrero was released on conditions.

According to the charging documents, in August 2026, a cooperating witness allegedly met with Gomez-Santana outside a restaurant in Pawtucket, R.I. and purchased approximately 250 grams of cocaine. Ahead of that sale, it is alleged that Gomez-Santana was seen meeting with a black Mercedes registered to Marrero.

A few weeks later, the cooperating witness allegedly arranged to meet with Gomez-Santana again, this time to buy approximately 1.5 kilograms of cocaine. On Sept. 29, 2026, Gomez-Santana allegedly met the cooperating witness in the parking lot of a shopping plaza in Taunton, Mass., before directing the cooperating witness to a gas station in Berkley, Mass. There, Gomez-Santana allegedly met with Marrero, who handed Gomez-Santana a bag containing approximately 1.5 kilograms of cocaine. It is alleged that Gomez-Santana then provided the cocaine to the cooperating witness in exchange for cash.

The charges of conspiracy to distribute and distribution of 500 grams or more of cocaine each provide for a sentence of no less than five years and up to 40 years in prison, at least four years and up to a lifetime of supervised release and a fine of up to $5 million. Due to a prior conviction for conspiracy to distribute drugs (for which he was sentenced to 90 months), Gomez-Santana faces an enhanced maximum penalty of penalty of life, with a mandatory sentence of at least 10 years in prison, at least eight years and up to a lifetime of supervised release and a fine of up to $8 million. Sentences are imposed by a federal district court judge based upon the U.S. Sentencing Guidelines and statutes which govern the determination of a sentence in a criminal case.

United States Attorney Leah B. Foley and Thomas Greco, Special Agent in Charge of the Bureau of Alcohol, Tobacco, Firearms & Explosives made the announcement. Valuable assistance was provided by the Massachusetts State Police and the Pawtucket (R.I.) and Bridgewater (Mass.) Police Departments. Assistant U.S. Attorney John J. Reynolds III of the Organized Crime & Gang Unit is prosecuting the cases.

The details contained in the charging documents are allegations. The defendants are presumed innocent unless and until proven guilty beyond a reasonable doubt in a court of law.

This case is part of Operation Take Back America a nationwide initiative that marshals the full resources of the Department of Justice to repel the invasion of illegal immigration, achieve the total elimination of cartels and transnational criminal organizations, and protect our communities from the perpetrators of violent crime.

Defense and Aerospace Contractors ILC Dover and ILC Astrospace Agree to Pay $13M to Resolve Cybersecurity Fraud Allegations
Defense and aerospace companies ILC Dover LP and ILC Astrospace LLC, of Frederica, Delaware, have agreed to pay $13 million to resolve allegations that they violated the False Claims Act by failing to comply with cybersecurity requirements in their contracts with the Department of the Army, the Missile Defense Agency, and the National Aeronautics and Space Administration (NASA).
“To protect sensitive information from cyber threats, defense and aerospace contractors must comply with the cybersecurity requirements in their federal contracts and subcontracts,” said Assistant Attorney General Brett A. Shumate of the Justice Department’s Civil Division. “We will continue our efforts to hold accountable government contractors and subcontractors that fail to meet their cybersecurity commitments.”
Today’s settlement resolves allegations that from January 2018 to October 2024, ILC Dover and ILC Astrospace (collectively, ILC) submitted false or fraudulent claims for payment on contracts with the Army, Missile Defense Agency, and NASA, and that those claims were false or fraudulent because ILC knew it had not complied with those contracts’ cybersecurity requirements. The settlement resolves allegations that:
- From February 2023 to October 2024, ILC allegedly used a third-party company to store controlled unclassified information in the cloud without requiring and ensuring that the third party met security requirements equivalent to the Federal Risk and Authorization Management Program (FedRAMP) Moderate baseline and complied with Department of Defense (DoD) requirements for cyber incident reporting, malicious software, media preservation and protection, access to additional information and equipment necessary for forensic analysis, and cyber incident damage assessment.
- From January 2018 to March 2022, and from September 2022 to October 2024, ILC allegedly did not develop, document, and periodically update a system security plan for each of its covered information systems, as required by DoD and NASA contracts, describing system boundaries, system environments of operation, how security requirements are implemented, and the relationships with or connections to other systems.
- From January 2018 to October 2024, ILC allegedly had not fully implemented all cybersecurity controls in National Institute of Standards and Technology (NIST) Special Publications (SP) 800-171 and 800-53, including controls that, if not implemented, could lead to significant exploitation of the network or exfiltration of controlled defense information and controls that, if not implemented, could have a specific and confined effect on the security of the network and its data.
- From January 2018 to May 2019, and from January 2022 to September 2024, ILC allegedly had not developed and implemented plans of action and milestones designed to correct deficiencies and reduce or eliminate vulnerabilities in ILC’s systems.
- From November 2020 to October 2024, ILC Astrospace allegedly had not submitted to DoD any current assessment of its implementation of NIST SP 800-171 cybersecurity controls, and ILC Dover allegedly had not submitted an assessment that was current, based on the entity’s review of a system security plan associated with covered contractor information systems, and conducted in accordance with the NIST SP 800-171 DoD Assessment Methodology.
“The best response to cyberattacks is to prevent them from happening in the first place,” said U.S. Attorney Benjamin L. Wallace for the District of Delaware. “The obligations that ILC violated exist to prevent bad actors from taking advantage of the United States’ technical innovation. My office is committed to ensuring that cybersecurity requirements in contracts are honored and that America’s leadership in aerospace is protected.”
“Cybersecurity lapses place critical defense information at risk,” said Acting Special Agent in Charge Jessica Herrington of the Department of Defense Office of Inspector General, Defense Criminal Investigative Service (DCIS), Northeast Field Office. “DCIS remains committed to ensuring that companies entrusted with sensitive data fully meet the security obligations outlined in their federal contracts. This settlement reflects our continued efforts to safeguard the Department of Defense’s information and hold contractors accountable when they fail to uphold required cybersecurity standards.”
“This case should send a clear message to anyone conducting business with the Department of the Army: If you engage in fraudulent or illegal activity, the Department of the Army Criminal Investigation Division (CID) will vigorously pursue those responsible and work tirelessly to bring them to justice,” said Special Agent in Charge Joel Kirch, of Army CID’s Northeast Field Office.
“Strict compliance with federal cybersecurity standards is non-negotiable for any company doing business with NASA,” said Robert Steinau, Assistant Inspector General for Investigations at the NASA Office of Inspector General. “Those who jeopardize America’s space program by ignoring government protocols will incur steep financial penalties. We are grateful to whistleblowers who do right by reporting these wrongs.”
The settlement resolves a lawsuit filed under the whistleblower provisions of the False Claims Act, which permit private parties to sue on behalf of the government when they believe that a defendant has submitted false claims for government funds and receive a share of any recovery. The settlement in this case provides for the whistleblower, Philip Root, ILC’s former Director of Cybersecurity, to receive a $2.35 million share of the settlement amount. The qui tam case is captioned United States ex rel. Root v. ILC Dover LP, et al., No. 25-cv-70 (D. Del.).
This year the Administration launched the Task Force to Eliminate Fraud and the National Fraud Enforcement Division to enhance the Administration’s war on fraud, waste, and abuse in federal programs. When unscrupulous actors exploit these programs for their own financial gain, they defraud the government, harm the people these programs are designed to aid and protect, and undermine American businesses that play by the rules. The Civil Division’s FCA enforcement plays a critical role in combatting such fraudulent schemes, recovering billions of dollars for the American taxpayers, and holding wrongdoers accountable. FCA matters will continue to be on the forefront of the battle against fraud, and the Civil Division’s FCA work will support and advance the mission of the Task Force to Eliminate Fraud and the National Fraud Enforcement Division.
The settlement announced today was the result of a coordinated effort between the Civil Division’s Commercial Litigation Branch, Fraud Section and the U.S. Attorney’s Office for the District of Delaware, with assistance from NASA OIG, the Defense Criminal Investigative Service, Army CID’s Northeast Field Office, the Navy Criminal Investigative Service, the Air Force Office of Special Investigations, and the General Services Administration Office of Inspector General.
The matter was handled by Assistant Director Christopher Terranova in the Civil Division’s Commercial Litigation Branch (Fraud Section) and Assistant U.S. Attorneys Dylan Steinberg and Jacob Laksin for the District of Delaware.
The claims resolved by the settlement are allegations only and there has been no determination of liability.
