WASHINGTON — The U.S. Small Business Administration is reminding eligible businesses, private nonprofit organizations, and residents in Washington of the Nov. 23 deadline to apply for low-interest federal disaster loans to offset physical damage caused by the Chelan Hills wildfire occurring July 4 – 10.
The declaration covers the Washington counties of Chelan, Douglas, Grant, Kittitas, and Okanogan.
Businesses and nonprofits are eligible to apply for physical disaster loans and may borrow up to $2 million to repair or replace disaster-damaged or destroyed real estate, machinery, and equipment, inventory, and other business assets.
Homeowners and renters are eligible to apply for home and personal property loans and may borrow up to $100,000 to replace or repair personal property, such as clothing, furniture, cars, and appliances. Homeowners may apply for up to $500,000 to replace or repair their primary residence.
Applicants may also be eligible for a loan increase of up to 20% of their physical damage, as verified by SBA, for mitigation purposes. Eligible mitigation improvements may include strengthening structures to protect against fire damage, upgrading to wind rated garage doors, and installing a safe room or storm shelter to help protect property and occupants from future damage.
“One distinct advantage of SBA’s disaster loan program is the opportunity to fund upgrades reducing the risk of future damage,” said Chris Stallings, Associate Administrator of the Office of Disaster Recovery at SBA. “I encourage businesses and homeowners to work with contractors and mitigation professionals to improve their disaster readiness while taking advantage of our physical damage loans.”
The SBA’s Economic Injury Disaster Loan program is available to eligible small businesses, small agricultural cooperatives, and private nonprofit organizations — including faith-based organizations — impacted by financial losses directly related to this disaster. The SBA is unable to provide disaster loans to agricultural producers, farmers, or ranchers, except for aquaculture enterprises.
Interest rates can be as low as 4% for businesses, 3.625% for nonprofits, and 2.875% for homeowners and renters with terms up to 30 years. Interest does not begin to accrue, and payments are not due until 12 months from the date of the first loan disbursement. The SBA determines eligibility and sets loan amounts and terms based on each applicant’s financial condition.
To apply online, visit sba.gov/disaster. Applicants may also call SBA’s National Support Network Center at (866) SBA-HELP or email disastercustomerservice@sba.gov for more information on SBA disaster assistance. For people who are deaf, hard of hearing, or have a speech disability, please dial 7-1-1 to access telecommunications relay services.
The filing deadline to submit applications for physical damage is Nov. 23. However, after the deadline has passed, there is a 60-day grace period in which SBA will accept applications. The deadline to return economic injury applications is June 22, 2027.
###
About the U.S. Small Business Administration
The U.S. Small Business Administration helps power the American dream of business ownership. As the only go-to resource and voice for small businesses backed by the strength of the federal government, the SBA empowers entrepreneurs and small business owners with the resources and support they need to start, grow, expand their businesses, or recover from a declared disaster. It delivers services through an extensive network of SBA field offices and partnerships with public and private organizations. To learn more, visit www.sba.gov.
title: SBA Relief Still Available to Washington Businesses, Private Nonprofits, Residents Affected by the Chelan Hills Wildfire

The Federal Maritime Commission (FMC) will host a research symposium on March 31, 2027, at its headquarters in Washington, D.C. This event will bring together scholars conducting research on demurrage and detention (DnD) practices and policies, as well as industry experts who will share insights regarding the use of DnD to incentivize cargo fluidity and velocity.
The symposium will foster research and discussion that can advance the understanding of DnD practices and their broader economic and operational implications for freight fluidity. The symposium will focus on the following overarching research question: What economic theories or quantifiable frameworks can be developed and used to evaluate the relationships among compensatory costs, DnD charge levels, and the behavioral responses necessary to effectively incentivize cargo movement and freight fluidity?
The FMC is now accepting submission from individuals interested in sharing their papers examining the policies and effects of DnD. The Commission especially encourages the submission of papers that develop and/or evaluate methodologies for setting DnD charges above compensatory costs in order to maintain and demonstrate an effective incentive. Papers may also develop or examine methodologies to assess behavioral responses to DnD charges and how those responses can be deployed to improve cargo velocity and freight fluidity.
Key dates
- Deadline for submissions – February 15, 2027
- Notification to author(s) – March 1, 2027
- Registration opens and agenda announced – March 1, 2027
- Research symposium – March 31, 2027
The research symposium will focus on the following key themes and questions:
Overall incentivizing mechanism:
- Establish a quantifiable economic framework for determining whether, and by how much, DnD charges must differ from actual compensatory costs to effectively incentivize the desired behavioral responses.
- Identify controllable and uncontrollable factors associated with DnD and evaluate how these factors affect charge levels, compensatory costs, and incentive effectiveness.
DnD charges:
- What factors impact the effectiveness of DnD charges as financial incentives?
- Examine how DnD terms and rates are negotiated and determine how contractual relationships, the Incoterms, and/or government holds influence the level and structure of DnD charges.
- Examine decision-making alignment across relevant parties, including whether the party that controls the relevant operational behavior is consistently the party that bears the financial consequences of DnD charges.
Compensatory costs:
- How should compensatory costs associated with DnD be identified, measured, and quantified?
- How can one deploy a quantifiable framework for compensatory costs, including actual costs and opportunity costs, associated with DnD and identify the factors that influence those costs?
Behavioral changes:
- What is the demonstrated relationship between increases in DnD charges and incremental improvements in the desired behavior, and at what point do diminishing returns occur?
- Examine how behavioral responses to DnD incentives translate into improvements in cargo velocity and overall freight fluidity.
If you are interested in submitting a paper, please send an executive summary, extended abstract, or completed paper by February 15, 2027, to Grace Wang at WWang@fmc.gov. You will receive an email confirming receipt of your submission. Preference to participate in the symposium will be given to completed papers.
Accepted participants should expect to receive notification by March 1, 2027. For those interested in attending the conference as audience members, registration will open March 1, 2027. This symposium will be held at FMC Headquarters: 800 North Capitol Street, N.W. Washington, D.C., 20573. For more information or questions, please contact Grace Wang at WWang@fmc.gov and Melina Reilly at MReilly@fmc.gov.
title: FMC will Host a Research Symposium on Demurrage and Detention

The Army has conducted ceremonies throughout its history to celebrate special occasions, like a new commander taking the reins of a unit.
Brig. Gen. Jeremy Wilson assumed command of the Army Training Center and Fort Jackson in one such ceremony held Oct. 30 at Victory Field on post.
“Thank you for being here today as we welcome the Wilson family to Fort Jackson,” said Lt. Gen. Johnny K. Davis, commander of the U.S. Army Recruiting Command, who presided over the ceremony. “I want to recognize Brig. Gen. Jeremy Wilson’s incredible family, his wife Marti, their children and the loved ones here with us today.”
The ceremony marked the placing of trust on the shoulders “of a proven combat leader, an exceptional trainer, and a leader of character who understands what it takes to build readiness from the ground up,” Davis said.
Davis added Wilson has his total confidence.
“You’ve got an incredible team of superstars behind you, and I know … you’re going to crush it,” he said.
Commanding a unit like the Army Training Center takes a commitment from the whole family, said Davis, who leads the organization that runs the Army’s force generation pipeline.
It is “a team sport and a family commitment,” he said while welcoming the Wilsons to the team. “We know Jeremy wouldn’t do it; wouldn’t be standing here without the strength and love behind him from this great family.”
Wilson, who started his Army career as an armor officer upon graduation from the Citadel in 1996, said he is “humbled and honored” to take command.
“Fort Jackson holds a special place in our Army,” he said during the ceremony. “Our mission is fundamental to America’s national defense. Bottom line, we make American Soldiers. Every day young men and women arrive here as civilians to begin their transformation into disciplined, capable, members of our profession.
“The responsibility we carry is profound, and the standard we uphold must always reflect the trust our nation place in us.”
Wilson took command of a post where a roughly half of America’s Soldiers are forged.
“You cannot help but be inspired by what Fort Jackson represents to our nation,” Davis added. “Fifty percent of all Soldiers, active, Reserve and National Guard, who enter the U.S. Army begin their journey right here at Fort Jackson. Think about that for a second – half of our entire fighting force is forged on this ground.”
“This is where civilian volunteers who raised their right hand to transform into disciplined, tough American war fighters,” he added. “Fort Jackson is building Soldiers who are prepared, adaptable, and ready for anything our nation calls on them to do, whether that is deterring conflict, deploying overseas, or answering the call in times of crisis.
“That standard is carried out every single day by absolute best of the best: our drill sergeants, instructors, cadre and Department of the Army Civilians.”
Wilson said he was committed to the mission and will lead with purpose.
“My commitment to all of you is to lead with purpose, listen with humility, make decisions with integrity, and keep us focused on readiness, people, and excellence,” he said.
Fort Jackson’s 55th commanding general has deployed multiple times and was previously the deputy commanding general for the Combined Arms Center-Training at Fort Leavenworth, Kansas.
title: Fort Jackson welcomes Wilson as 55th commanding general

Agency recognized for continued investment in veteran hiring and support
WASHINGTON — As Veterans Day approaches, U.S. Customs and Border Protection recognizes the more than 18,000 people who continue serving the nation as part of approximately one-quarter of the agency’s workforce. We would also like to market the release to the surrounding military bases once approved.
Veterans serve throughout the agency as U.S. Border Patrol agents, CBP officers, Air and Marine agents, criminal investigators, mission-support professionals and agency leaders. In fiscal year 2026, CBP hired 1,539 veterans, representing 18.5 percent of all new hires, and will participate in multiple Veteran career fairs throughout the country.
“CBP is proud to recognize the veterans across our workforce whose service to our nation did not end when they left the military,” said CBP Commissioner Rodney S. Scott. “Their professionalism, teamwork, and sense of duty strengthen our mission every day. This Veterans Day, we thank all veterans for their service and their continued contributions to our country.”
Each year, CBP is recognized as a leading employer for veterans. This year, U.S. Veterans Magazine recognized CBP for its commitment to recruiting, hiring and supporting veterans and transitioning service members. The Department of War also recognized CBP for fostering supportive work environments for Reserve and National Guard service members.
CBP’s commitment extends beyond recruitment. Through the CBP Veteran Support Program, employees and their families receive assistance navigating employment benefits, connecting with Department of Veterans Affairs resources, and accessing mental, physical and emotional health support. A worldwide network of approximately 300 coordinators helped 1,151 employees obtain an estimated $18 million in direct compensation during fiscal year 2024.
CBP also supports transitioning service members through the Department of War SkillBridge Internship Program, which provides practical, pre-separation work experience in non-law-enforcement career fields. The agency offers 167 internship opportunities across 25 states, the District of Columbia and Puerto Rico. In fiscal year 2026, CBP hosted 54 SkillBridge interns, 13 of whom were subsequently hired into permanent CBP positions.
For more information about careers with U.S. Customs and Border Protection, visit the CBP Careers link.

Memphis, TN – Two aliens have been indicted in the Western District of Tennessee and are facing federal charges for illegally voting in federal elections. D. Michael Dunavant, United States Attorney for the Western District of Tennessee, announced the unsealing of the indictments today.

As alleged in the indictments, two aliens have been charged for illegally voting in federal elections in the Western District of Tennessee:

Cesar Sanchez Correa, 44, a citizen of Mexico , allegedly illegally voted in Haywood County, TN in the 2024 election held in part for the purpose of electing a candidate for President, Vice President, Member of the United States Senate, or Member of the United States House of Representatives, and allegedly falsely and willfully represented himself to be a citizen of the United States in a Tennessee voter registration application in order to vote in a federal, state, or local election. Sanchez Correa is charged with one count of unlawful voting by an alien, in violation of 18 U.S.C. § 611.

Andreas Van Der Werf, 62, a citizen of Germany , allegedly illegally voted in Fayette County, TN in both the 2022 and 2024 elections held in part for the purpose of electing a candidate for President, Vice President, Member of the United States Senate, or Member of the United States House of Representatives, and allegedly falsely and willfully represented himself to be a citizen of the United States in a Tennessee voter registration application in order to vote in a federal, state, or local election. Van Der Werf is charged with two counts of unlawful voting by an alien, in violation of 18 U.S.C. § 611.

U.S. Attorney D. Michael Dunavant said, “The law is clear: Only American citizens may vote in American elections. Every American citizen must be able to have their vote counted without it being stolen because of fraudulent or ineligible voters. Illegal voting is a crime and will be aggressively prosecuted by the Department of Justice to protect the integrity of the election process.”

“Protecting the integrity of our elections is a responsibility HSI takes seriously,” said HSI Nashville Special Agent in Charge Dennis M. Fetting. “With our partners, we will continue to investigate alleged violations of federal election laws and support efforts to uphold the foundations of our democracy.”

These cases were investigated by the Federal Bureau of Investigation and Homeland Security Investigations, with the assistance of the Tennessee Secretary of State’s Office.

Assistant United States Attorneys from the U.S. Attorney's Office Special Prosecutions Unit will be prosecuting the cases on behalf of the United States.

The charges and allegations contained in the indictment are merely accusations of criminal conduct, not evidence. The defendants are presumed innocent unless and until proven guilty beyond a reasonable doubt and convicted through due process of law.

###

For more information, please contact our Media Relations Team at USATNW.Media@usdoj.gov . Follow the U.S. Attorney’s Office on Facebook or on X at @WDTNNews for office news and updates.
title: Two Aliens in West Tennessee Charged with Illegal Voting in Federal Elections

ROCHESTER, N.Y.-U.S. Attorney Michael DiGiacomo announced today that Matthew David Marvin, 38, of Perinton, NY, was arrested and charged by criminal complaint with production and attempted production, receipt and possession of child pornography, which carry a mandatory minimum penalty of 15 years in prison and a maximum of 30 years.

According to the criminal complaint, on June 7, 2026, the Monroe County Sheriff’s Office was alerted to nude photographs of a 12 year old minor victim found on a laptop computer, which was taken into the custody by the Sheriff’s Office. Subsequent investigation traced the laptop and the photographs to Marvin. The complaint states that the videos were taken using a camera stored in the ceiling of a bathroom in Marvin’s home. On June 19, 2026, during a forensic analysis of the laptop, investigators recovered five video files depicting the same bathroom and females using the bathroom, one of whom appeared to be a naked minor.

On June 26, 2026, a search warrant was executed at Marvin’s residence, during which investigators seized numerous electronic items, including a desktop computer, two hard drives and Marvin’s cell phone. A forensic analysis of the electronic items recovered several thousand images and video files consistent with being recorded from a camera inside of a bathroom. The images and videos appeared to be recorded over a nearly three year period of time. Additional images and videos of child pornography obtained via the internet, as well as search terms and websites associated with child pornography, were located on the devices.

Marvin made an initial appearance before U.S. Magistrate Judge Mark W. Pedersen and was held pending a detention hearing on November 3, 2026.

The case is being prosecuted by Assistant U.S. Attorney Katelyn M. Hartford. The complaint is the result of an investigation by the Monroe County Sheriff's Office, under the direction of Sheriff Todd Baxter and Homeland Security Investigations, under the direction of Acting Special Agent-in-Charge Anthony Patrone.

The fact that a defendant has been charged with a crime is merely an accusation and the defendant is presumed innocent until and unless proven guilty.

title: Perinton man arrested, charged with production of child pornography

Hoyer Statement on the Beginning of the 2027 Open Enrollment Period
WASHINGTON, DC – Congressman Steny H. Hoyer (MD-05) released the following statement to mark the beginning of the enrollment period for health insurance coverage in 2027:
"I encourage all Marylanders to visit MarylandHealthConnection.gov to explore their options and enroll in a high-quality, affordable health-care plan that works best for them. Even families with existing plans should visit Maryland Health Connection to review their coverage and ensure that it meets their needs for the coming year.
“Sixteen years ago, I was proud to help to secure House passage of the Affordable Care Act, but that achievement is now once again under threat. Since taking office last year, President Trump and Congressional Republicans have made devastating cuts to health-care access and affordability, gutting over $1 trillion from Medicaid and the Affordable Care Act. Presently, millions of Americans are struggling to choose between rising health-care premiums and putting food on the table because of these Republican cuts. With 152,000 Marylanders in jeopardy of losing their coverage by 2028, it is critical, now more than ever, that we work to fix our broken health-care system. If returned to the Majority, House Democrats are committed to expanding access and improving coverage while lowering health-care costs for all Americans.
“Every Marylander ought to be able to access high-qualify and affordable health care, and for many families that begins by visiting MarylandHealthConnection.gov.”

NORFOLK, Va. – A Chesapeake woman pled guilty to wire fraud in relation to falsely representing her credentials to provide hair and tattoo removal by laser.

According to court documents, Hayley Nicole Atwood, 33, was licensed by the Virginia Department of Professional and Occupational Regulation as a basic esthetician. Beginning in at least 2017, Atwood consistently falsely purported to be a master esthetician to colleagues and potential customers. Under Virginia law, master estheticians may perform more advanced procedures such as laser hair removal or laser tattoo removal, but only if properly trained and supervised by a licensed physician or physician assistant.

Atwood owned and operated esthetics spas in Chesapeake, Virginia, and Elizabeth City, North Carolina. In March and April of 2021, Atwood purchased two Spectrum Laser devices for her spas. Atwood employed a medical director from December 2019 through July 2021 and a second medical director from July 2021 through November 2022. Neither medical director ever supervised or authorized Atwood or anyone at her business to perform laser tattoo removal. The second director supervised laser hair removal but never evaluated Atwood or her staff or saw her patients. Atwood consistently advertised, offered, and performed laser tattoo and hair removal. Several of Atwood’s clients suffered injury as a result of her laser treatments, including burning and scarring.

Atwood is scheduled to be sentenced on March 5, 2027, and faces up to 20 years in prison. A federal district court judge will determine any sentence after considering the U.S. Sentencing Guidelines and other statutory factors.

Theophani K. Stamos, First Assistant U.S. Attorney for the Eastern District of Virginia; Marie Maguire, Special Agent in Charge, FDA Office of Criminal Investigations, Metro Washington Field Office; and Col. Jeffrey S. Katz, Superintendent of Virginia State Police, made the announcement after U.S. Magistrate Judge Douglas E. Miller accepted the plea.

Assistant U.S. Attorneys Kristen S. Taylor and Rebecca Gantt are prosecuting the case.

Related court documents and information are located on the website of the District Court for the Eastern District of Virginia or on PACER by searching for Case No. 2:26-cr-83.
title: Chesapeake esthetician pleads guilty in laser treatment case

Homeland Security Task Force Investigation Yields Federal Charges for 13 Aliens Charged with Fraud Against the United States
ORLANDO, Fla. — Thirteen aliens from Brazil and Cuba have been charged by indictment for their roles in a conspiracy to defraud the United States and other aliens. The charges include conspiracy to commit wire fraud, wire fraud, visa fraud, unlawful employment of aliens, and marriage fraud. United States Attorney Gregory W. Kehoe made the announcement. U.S. Citizenship and Immigration Services provided valuable support to the investigation.
Vagner Sorares De Almeida, 54; Juliana Colucci, 47; Lucas Felipe Trindade Silva, 34; and Ronaldo De Campos, 35, are each charged with one count of conspiracy to commit wire fraud and two counts of wire fraud. They are also charged with four counts of conspiracy to commit visa fraud, one count of conspiracy to commit marriage fraud, and one count of unlawful employment of aliens.
Erick Bruno Goncalves De Assis Pinto, 34; Nathalia Da Costa Ferreira, 43; Nathalia Gomes Ciriaco, 29; and Kelen Cristina Da Silva, 37, are each charged with charged with one count of conspiracy to commit wire fraud, two counts of wire fraud, and four counts of conspiracy to commit visa fraud.
Issac Antonio Narvaez, 69, is charged with three counts of conspiracy to commit marriage fraud.
Ronay Castillo Salazar, 51; Rebeca Aldama Garcia, 40; Mijail Cabera Nunez, 52; and Lorraine Soares Oliverira, 32, are each charged with one count of conspiracy to commit marriage fraud.
According to court records, from Aug. 18, 2023, through April 20, 2026, Vagner Sorares De Almeida owned and operated a corporate entity registered in Florida called Legacy Imigra Solutions LLC (“Legacy”). Juliana Colucci, Lucas Felipe Trindade Silva, Nathalia Da Costa Ferreira, Nathalia Gomes Ciriaco, Ronaldo De Campos, Erick Bruno Goncalves De Assis Pinto, and Kelen Cristina Da Silva were employees of the company. Legacy falsely purported to be a professional establishment employed by immigration experts and attorneys who could assist individuals with immigration-related legal work. It was part of the conspiracy to give false, inaccurate, and incomplete legal and immigration advice to prospective clients to induce them to retain Legacy’s services. Legacy would falsify immigration documents to fraudulently obtain immigration status and benefits for their clients.
The defendants also engaged in a regular practice of hiring aliens knowing that the individuals were unauthorized for employment in the United States. Vagner Sorares De Almeida, Juliana Colucci, Ronay Castillo Salazar, Rebeca Aldama Garcia, Mijail Cabera Nunez, Lorraine Soares Oliverira, and Issac Antonio Narvaez also conspired to commit marriage fraud.
If convicted, each count of conspiracy to commit wire fraud and wire fraud carries a maximum penalty of 20 years’ imprisonment. The conspiracy to commit visa fraud offenses are each punishable up to 10 years’ imprisonment. The maximum penalty for conspiracy to commit marriage fraud is 5 years in federal prison, and unlawful employment of aliens carries a maximum penalty of 6 months’ imprisonment.
An indictment is merely a formal charge that a defendant has committed one or more violations of federal criminal law, and every defendant is presumed innocent unless, and until, proven guilty.
This case is being investigated by U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement’s Homeland Security Investigations (Orlando, Tampa, and Brasilia) and Enforcement and Removal Operations, IRS Criminal Investigation, the Department of Labor Office of Inspector General, the Department of Agriculture Office of Inspector General, USCIS, U.S. Customs and Border Protection, the U.S. Marshals Service, the Orange County Sheriff’s Office, Florida Highway Patrol, and the Florida Department of Law Enforcement. It is being prosecuted by Assistant United States Attorney Bianca Bansal.
To report suspected immigration benefit fraud or abuse to USCIS, please use the USCIS Tip Form.
For more information on USCIS and its programs, please visit USCIS.gov or follow us on X, Instagram, YouTube, Facebook and LinkedIn.
title: Homeland Security Task Force Investigation Yields Federal Charges for 13 Aliens Charged with Fraud Against the United States

Nine Charged as a Result of Homeland Security Task Force Investigation into Southeastern Connecticut Cocaine Trafficking
BRIDGEPORT, Conn. - David X. Sullivan, United States Attorney for the District of Connecticut, Jarod Forget, Special Agent in Charge of the Drug Enforcement Administration for New England, and Thomas A. Greco, Special Agent in Charge, ATF Boston Field Division, today announced that the following nine individuals have been charged by indictment with offenses related to the distribution of cocaine and crack cocaine in southeastern Connecticut:
MICHAEL SMITH, also known as “Miz,” 53, of Lisbon
ANTHONY GOMEZ, also known as “Jungle,” 46, of Norwich
ROBERT DURAN, 46, of Mount Vernon, New York
DEONNA WHITE, 48, of Norwich
ROCKY LAURENT, 48, of New London
SARAH BUTLER, 43, of Norwich
HEATHER ROY, 44, of Canterbury
CORDELIA HARRIS, 49, of New London
KEITH NIVAL, 46, of New London
As alleged in court documents and statements made in court, a Homeland Security Task Force investigation, which has included court-authorized wiretaps, video surveillance, GPS tracking of vehicles, and numerous controlled purchases of narcotics, revealed that Smith supplied cocaine and crack to a network of redistributors in southeastern Connecticut. Laurent, Butler, Roy, Harris, and Nival purchased cocaine and crack from Smith and sold it in smaller quantities to their own customers.
It is further alleged that on October 8, 2026, investigators conducting surveillance at a parking lot in Clinton observed Smith, White, and Duran arrive in separate vehicles. Smith retrieved a reusable shopping bag from White’s vehicle and then drove to another area of the lot to meet Duran. Smith gave the bag to Duran who then placed a box in the back of Smith’s vehicle. Smith, White, and Duran were arrested after a search of the box revealed approximately 10 kilograms of cocaine, and a search of the shopping bag revealed more than $170,000 in cash. Butler was also arrested on October 8, after a search of her residence in the Taftville section of Norwich revealed narcotics and drug packaging materials. Investigators also searched two of Smith’s vehicles and found cocaine and crack cocaine packaged for redistribution in one vehicle, and a firearm and more than 200 rounds of ammunition in the other vehicle.
Gomez, Roy, Harris, and Nival were arrested on October 15, 2026, and Laurent has been in state custody since September 23, 2026. Smith, Gomez, Duran, and Nival have been detained since their arrests.
On October 27, 2026, a grand jury in New Haven returned a superseding indictment charging each of the defendants with conspiracy to distribute and to possess with intent to distribute cocaine. If convicted of this charge, based on the quantity of cocaine attributed to each defendant, Smith, Gomez, Duran, White, and Laurent face a mandatory minimum term of imprisonment of 10 years and a maximum term of imprisonment of life; Butler, Harris, and Roy face a mandatory minimum term of imprisonment of five years and a maximum term of imprisonment of 40 years; and Nival faces a maximum term of imprisonment of 20 years.
The indictment also charges Gomez with three counts of possession with intent to distribute, and distribution of, 28 grams or more of cocaine base (“crack”), an offense that carries a mandatory minimum term of imprisonment of five years and a maximum term of imprisonment of 40 years on each count; Smith and Duran with possession with intent to distribute five kilograms or more of cocaine, an offense that carries a mandatory minimum term of imprisonment of 10 years and a maximum term of imprisonment of life; and Smith with unlawful possession of ammunition by a felon, an offense that carries a maximum term of imprisonment of 15 years.
The indictment also seeks the forfeiture of $196,353 in cash and five vehicles seized during the investigation.
U.S. Attorney Sullivan stressed that an indictment is not evidence of guilt. Charges are only allegations, and each defendant is presumed innocent unless and until proven guilty beyond a reasonable doubt.
This matter is being investigated by the Drug Enforcement Administration and the Bureau of Alcohol, Tobacco, Firearms, and Explosives, with assistance from the Connecticut State Police. The case is being prosecuted by Assistant U.S. Attorneys Christopher Lembo, Justyn Stokely, and Natasha Freismuth.
This prosecution is part of the Homeland Security Task Force (HSTF) initiative established by Executive Order 14159, Protecting the American People Against Invasion. The HSTF is a whole-of-government partnership dedicated to eliminating criminal cartels, foreign gangs, transnational criminal organizations, and human smuggling and trafficking rings operating in the United States and abroad. Through historic interagency collaboration, the HSTF directs the full might of United States law enforcement toward identifying, investigating, and prosecuting the full spectrum of crimes committed by these organizations, which have long fueled violence and instability within our borders. In performing this work, the HSTF places special emphasis on investigating and prosecuting those engaged in child trafficking or other crimes involving children. The HSTF further utilizes all available tools to prosecute and remove the most violent criminal aliens from the United States.
HSTF New Haven comprises agents and officers from the FBI, DEA, HSI, ATF, U.S. Postal Inspection Service, Internal Revenue Service – Criminal Investigation, U.S. Department of Transportation – Office of Inspector General, U.S. Department of Labor – Office of Inspector General, U.S. Department of Commerce – Bureau of Industry and Security’s Office of Export Enforcement, and Connecticut State Police, with prosecutions led by the U.S. Attorney’s Office for the District of Connecticut.
title: Nine Charged as a Result of Homeland Security Task Force Investigation into Southeastern Connecticut Cocaine Trafficking

Protecting Kids from Lead: Federal Leaders Visit Philadelphia Hospital to Promote Prevention and Safe Housing
EPA, HHS, and HUD Regional Administrators Visit St. Christopher’s Hospital for Children to Highlight Lead Poisoning Prevention, Testing, and Safe Housing
PHILADELPHIA - Regional Administrators from U.S. Environmental Protection Agency (EPA), U.S. Department of Health and Human Services (HHS), and U.S. Department of Housing and Urban Development (HUD) visited St. Christopher’s Hospital for Children in Philadelphia today to underscore a shared commitment to protecting children from lead exposure.
The visit highlighted the importance of public education, housing remediation, clinical screening, and safe drinking water as part of a coordinated federal effort to help families identify and reduce lead risks in their homes and immediate surroundings. Under the message “Get the Facts and Get Your Home Tested,” the agencies emphasized that parents and caregivers can take practical steps to protect children from lead in paint, dust, soil, and drinking water.
“Every child deserves to grow up in a safe environment, free from the preventable harms of lead exposure,” said EPA Mid-Atlantic Regional Administrator Amy Van Blarcom-Lackey. “At EPA, we are focused on the facts: replacing lead service lines, supporting clean and safe drinking water, and giving families the tools they need to understand and reduce risks in their homes. This is about protecting children today and preventing harm for generations to come.”
The visit also highlighted the role of federal investment in addressing legacy infrastructure and older housing stock, especially in communities that have historically faced higher environmental and health burdens. EPA is working with local and state partners to replace lead service lines and support clean drinking water in schools, childcare facilities, and residential systems across the region.
“Childhood lead poisoning is a public health issue that we can and must prevent,” said HHS Regional Director Tatiana Villa. “Clinical screening, family education, and early intervention are critical pieces of the solution. By working with EPA and HUD, we can better connect families to the information and resources they need to protect their children’s health.”
The agencies also stressed the importance of housing-related protections, including lead paint abatement and remediation in older homes, apartments, and public housing.
“Safe housing is a foundation for healthy families,” said Joseph DeFelice, HUD Assistant Deputy Secretary for Field Policy and Management and Region III Administrator. “HUD is committed to working with our federal partners and local leaders to reduce lead hazards in homes and neighborhoods, especially in communities with older housing stock. Collaboration is essential if we want to make real progress and ensure that every child has a chance to thrive.”
Together, the agencies are aligning environmental protection, housing mitigation, and health screening to address childhood lead poisoning from multiple angles. The joint visit underscored the power of interagency collaboration and the importance of focusing federal attention and resources on communities where children may face elevated risks.
The visit at St. Christopher’s Hospital for Children reflected a shared federal commitment to protecting children’s health, supporting community education, and ensuring that families have access to actionable tools and trusted information.
“At St. Christopher’s, keeping children healthy has been our mission for more than 150 years. When we help families prevent lead exposure, we are protecting children's ability to learn, grow, and reach their full potential. We are proud to stand alongside our community and public health partners in this important effort to keep kids safe,” said Claire Alminde, President, St. Christopher's Hospital for Children.
Families seeking to learn more about lead risks in their homes can:
- Get their home tested for lead hazards
- Check whether their drinking water service line may contain lead
- Talk with their health care provider about lead screening for children
- Use federal, state, and local resources to reduce exposure risks

title: Protecting Kids from Lead: Federal Leaders Visit Philadelphia Hospital to Promote Prevention and Safe Housing

WASHINGTON — The U.S. Small Business Administration announced today the opening of Business Recovery Centers in the counties of Hinsdale and Lake, and a Disaster Loan Outreach Center in the county of Ouray to assist communities affected by the Elk Fire occurring July 9 – Oct. 1, the Willow Fire occurring June 28- Sept. 16, and wildfires, flooding, and mudslides occurring June 27 – July 29.
Beginning Tues., Nov. 3, SBA customer service representatives will be on hand at the BRCs in Lake City and Leadville, and on Mon., Nov. 9, SBA customer service representatives will be on hand at the DLOC in Ridgeway to answer questions and assist with the disaster loan application process. Walk-ins are welcome and in-person appointments can be scheduled in advance at appointment.sba.gov.
The centers’ hours of operation are as follows:
HINSDALE COUNTY
Business Recovery Center
Hinsdale County Administration Building
319 N. Henson St.
Lake City, CO  81235
Opens Tuesday, Nov. 3 at 1 p.m.
Tuesday - Friday, 9 a.m. – 6 p.m.
Closes permanently Friday, Nov.6 at 6 p.m.
LAKE COUNTY
Business Recovery Center
Lake County Public Library
1115 Harrison Ave.
Leadville, CO  80464
Opens Tuesday, Nov. 3 at 1 p.m.
Monday – Friday, 9 a.m. – 6 p.m.
Closes permanently Tuesday, Nov. 10 at 6 p.m.
OURAY COUNTY
Disaster Loan Outreach Center
Ouray County Fairgrounds
22739 US-550
Ridgway, CO  81432
Opens Monday, Nov. 9 at 1 p.m.
Closed Wednesday, Nov. 11, in observation of Veterans Day
Monday – Friday, 9 a.m. – 6 p.m.
Closes permanently Monday, Nov. 16 at 6 p.m.
“When disasters strike, SBA’s Disaster Loan Outreach Centers perform an important role by assisting small businesses and their communities,” said Chris Stallings, Associate Administrator of the Office of Disaster Recovery at the U.S. Small Business Administration. “At these centers, our SBA specialists help business owners and residents apply for disaster loans and learn about the full range of programs available to support their recovery.”
In Ouray County, businesses and nonprofits are eligible to apply for business physical disaster loans and may borrow up to $2 million to repair or replace disaster-damaged or destroyed real estate, machinery and equipment, inventory, and other business assets.
Homeowners and renters in Ouray County are eligible to apply for home and personal property loans and may borrow up to $100,000 to replace or repair personal property, such as clothing, furniture, cars, and appliances. Homeowners may apply for up to $500,000 to replace or repair their primary residence.
Applicants may be eligible for a loan increase of up to 20% of their verified physical damage, for mitigation purposes. Eligible mitigation improvements may include insulating pipes, walls and attics, weather stripping doors and windows, and installing storm windows to help protect property and occupants from future disasters.
The SBA’s Economic Injury Disaster Loan program is available to small businesses, small agricultural cooperatives, and private nonprofit organizations — including faith‑based organizations — with financial losses directly related to the Elk and Willow Fire disasters. The SBA is unable to provide disaster loans to agricultural producers, farmers, or ranchers, except for small aquaculture enterprises.
EIDLs are available for working capital needs caused by the disaster and are available even if the small business or private nonprofit did not suffer any physical damage. The loans may be used to pay fixed debts, payroll, accounts payable, and other bills which could not be paid due to the disaster.
Interest rates are as low as 4% for businesses, 3.625% for nonprofits, and 2.875% for homeowners and renters with terms up to 30 years. Interest does not begin to accrue, and payments are not due until 12 months from the date of the first loan disbursement. The SBA determines eligibility and sets loan amounts and terms based on each applicant’s financial condition.
To apply online, visit sba.gov/disaster. Applicants may also call SBA’s National Support Network Center at (866) SBA-HELP or email disastercustomerservice@sba.gov for more information on SBA disaster assistance. For people who are deaf, hard of hearing, or have a speech disability, please dial 7-1-1 to access telecommunications relay services.
The deadline to return physical damage applications for Ouray County is Dec. 22. The deadline to return economic injury applications for all three declarations is July 23, 2027.
###
About the U.S. Small Business Administration
The U.S. Small Business Administration helps power the American dream of business ownership. As the only go-to resource and voice for small businesses backed by the strength of the federal government, the SBA empowers entrepreneurs and small business owners with the resources and support they need to start, grow, expand their businesses, or recover from a declared disaster. It delivers services through an extensive network of SBA field offices and partnerships with public and private organizations. To learn more, visit www.sba.gov.
title: SBA Opens Disaster Loan Outreach Center in Ridgeway and Business Recovery Centers in Lake City and Hinsdale

Ranking Member Scott Slams ED for Playing Games with Public Service Loan Forgiveness Program
WASHINGTON – Today, House Education and Workforce Ranking Member Robert C. “Bobby” Scott (VA-03) demanded answers from Department of Education (ED) Secretary Linda McMahon, following concerning reports from borrowers in the Public Service Loan Forgiveness (PSLF) program that several qualifying payments were erased from their accounts.
Established in 2007, PSLF offers loan forgiveness to public servants who work for a qualified employer for 10 years and make 120 payments toward their federal student loans. However, borrowers have recently reported that the number of PSLF-qualifying payments, tracked on a counter on the Office for Federal Student Aid’s (FSA’s) website, appeared incorrect. Despite acknowledging the data error, ED failed to provide detailed information on the cause of the error.
“Without additional information from the Department, borrowers cannot know whether changes to the PSLF qualifying payment count were the result of an error that will be fixed; if it is a decision that can be appealed; or if the statement reflects an unappealable decision made by this Administration. Without any additional information, borrowers are left in the dark as to why they must remain in repayment longer than the law requires. This is particularly concerning if a borrower believes they have met all the statutory and regulatory requirements to have their debt forgiven through the PSLF,” wrote Ranking Member Scott.
In his letter, Ranking Member Scott also emphasized that the qualifying payment-count errors come as the Department has not addressed the 88,000-application backlog in the PSLF buyback program and has eliminated affordable repayment plans, creating financial uncertainty and distress for student loan borrowers.
On Friday, October 30, 2026, the American Federation of Teachers (AFT), with support from Protect Borrowers, sued the Trump Administration, alleging it unlawfully blocked student loan forgiveness for tens of thousands of borrowers who qualify. The lawsuit, Weingarten v. McMahon, alleges ED Secretary McMahon mismanaged PSLF by incorrectly counting borrowers’ payment timelines and not awarding people credit for time served.

Reps Peters, Vargas, Levin, and Jacobs Back San Diego County Registrar of Voters Amid Trump Admin Probe for Voter Data
November 2, 2026 
San Diego, CA — Today, U.S. Representative Scott Peters (CA-50) led members of the San Diego Congressional delegation, Reps. Juan Vargas (CA-52), Mike Levin (CA-49), and Sara Jacobs (CA-51), in a letter to U.S. Attorney General Todd Blanche amid the Department of Justice’s (DOJ) attempt to sanction voter rolls across California, including in San Diego County’s Registrars of Voters (ROV). 
The DOJ demanded that San Diego’s ROV provide voter information for over 1,700 voters, including driver’s license numbers, Social Security numbers, and voter registration applications, within 48 hours, and withhold their ballots until their citizenship is confirmed. In its response, the County pushed back against several unsubstantiated claims and argued that the DOJ's probe violated several election laws. 
The Members' letter reinforced the County’s claims and acknowledged that California’s registrars follow all state and federal election laws, including citizenship attestation and database verification through the California Secretary of State. They argued that the DOJ’s letter cites no legal authority to direct county ballot administration and that it violates the National Voter Registration Act’s (NVRA) 90-day quiet period against systematically removing voters from the rolls. 
“The information requested by DOJ is intended to confirm the department’s unsubstantiated allegations of noncitizen voting in California,” the Members noted, also pointing to the data cited by DOJ, which the Agency itself conceded “may be outdated or incomplete.” 
The Members also stated that unverified fraud allegations do not give registrars authority to violate federal law by refusing to count the votes of people already deemed eligible. They added that the DOJ’s demand fails to explain who would determine citizenship status, how, or when, less than a week before Election Day. 
“The request from DOJ violates the NVRA, Voting Rights Act, California state law, and jeopardizes Californians’ constitutional right to vote,” the Members concluded, adding that “as Members of the California Congressional delegation, we commend the work of our state ROVs to ensure state and federal election laws are upheld.” 
Background: Over the past several weeks, the DOJ has escalated pressure on California before Election Day and made unsubstantiated claims that large numbers of illegal voters are on the rolls. Federal courts have repeatedly intervened and denied the Administration’s attempt to interfere. 
In May, California Attorney General Rob Bonta joined Rep. Peters’ podcast, 72 and Sunny, to debunk the myth of widespread voter fraud, discuss how California has pushed back against the attacks from the Trump Administration, and highlight how the State is enhancing voter security for the election. Watch the full episode here.

OPM Announces Opening of Applications for 2027–2028 White House Fellows Program
WASHINGTON, DC — The US Office of Personnel Management (OPM) today announced that applications are now open for the 2027–2028 class of White House Fellows, offering exceptional Americans a unique opportunity to serve at the highest levels of the federal government and help shape the future of our nation.
Established in 1964, the White House Fellows Program is one of the nation’s most prestigious leadership and public service programs. Each year, a select group of accomplished individuals from across the country is chosen to spend a year working alongside cabinet secretaries, senior White House staff, and other top government officials, gaining firsthand experience in federal leadership and policymaking.
“The White House Fellows Program represents an extraordinary opportunity for talented Americans to bring their experience, ideas, and leadership to public service,” OPM Director Scott Kupor said. “Some of our nation’s most accomplished leaders got their start as White House Fellows, and we want the next generation of innovators, problem-solvers, and public servants to see what they can contribute. If you’ve ever considered serving your country, this is an opportunity to step forward, make a meaningful impact, and help shape the future of government.”
"This program has a distinguished legacy of leadership and public service that reaches back more than six decades,” Executive Director of the President's Commission on White House Fellows Mary Sprowls said. “We encourage patriotic, highly-motivated, and exceptional Americans to consider applying or urge others to apply.”
Selected Fellows participate in a full-time, paid fellowship in Washington, DC, where they work directly with senior administration officials on consequential issues facing the nation. In addition to their professional assignments, Fellows participate in an intensive education program featuring candid discussions with distinguished leaders from the public and private sectors, as well as community service initiatives that strengthen their commitment to civic engagement.
Since its founding, nearly 900 Americans have participated in the program, including Chairman of the Joint Chiefs of Staff Dan Caine, former Secretary of State General Colin Powell, former Secretary of Transportation Elaine Chao, Pulitzer Prize-winning historian Doris Kearns Goodwin, and US Senators Bill Hagerty and Dan Sullivan. White House Fellows alumni have gone on to serve as military leaders, educators, entrepreneurs, scientists, nonprofit founders, and executives, united by a shared commitment to serving their communities and country.
Applications for the 2027–2028 White House Fellows class are open now. Interested candidates can learn more about the program and application process here.

LITTLE ROCK—A federal jury has convicted Beth Englade of conspiracy to commit sex trafficking of a minor. The trial, which spanned three days, ended on Thursday, October 29, 2026, with guilty a verdict for Englade, 36, of Little Rock. Jonathan D. Ross, United States Attorney for the Eastern District of Arkansas, announced the verdict.

Englade was indicted by a federal grand jury on December 7, 2022, and went to trial on one count of conspiracy to commit sex trafficking of a minor.

The evidence at trial proved that in February 2018, a 6-year-old child was taken to Arkansas Children’s Hospital due to symptoms that were later determined to be caused by several sexually transmitted diseases. The child was interviewed by an FBI forensic interviewer and disclosed that a man, later determined to be DeMarcus George, had raped her. The child also disclosed that another man, later determined to be Mario Waters, had also raped her in a hotel room.

Doctors at Arkansas Children’s Hospital determined that it was unlikely the child had obtained each sexually transmitted disease from the same offender and that there were likely multiple offenders. Officers obtained search warrants for George and Waters’ blood and urine. Results indicated that George and Waters tested positive for sexually transmitted diseases that the minor had contracted.

At trial, George testified that Englade assisted him in the trafficking of the minor, including renting hotel rooms where the trafficking took place and making the minor available. George also testified that Englade brought the minor with her when Englade was engaged in prostitution. Financial records presented at trial during the time in question proved Englade did in fact rent numerous hotel rooms. Numerous text messages detailing the relationship of George and Englade were also presented to the jury, including Englade promising George that she would not talk to the police.

Further evidence, including Englade’s phone records, confirmed her contacting numerous hotels. The jury also heard Englade’s statements to police, which contained numerous inconsistencies.

After deliberating for approximately three hours, the jury found Englade guilty of conspiracy to commit sex trafficking of a minor.

George and Waters were indicted for conspiracy to commit sex trafficking of a minor in 2019. George pleaded guilty on November 10, 2021, and was sentenced to life in prison on November 2, 2022. Waters pleaded guilty on September 29, 2021, and was sentenced to life in prison on March 13, 2023. Waters was killed a short time later while in custody in the Bureau of Prisons.

Englade will be sentenced at a later date. Englade’s charges carry a sentence of up to life imprisonment. There is no parole in the federal system.

This case was brought as part of Project Safe Childhood, a nationwide initiative to combat the growing epidemic of child sexual exploitation and abuse. Launched in May 2006 by the Department of Justice and led by the U.S. Attorney’s Offices and the Criminal Divisions Child Exploitation and Obscenity Section (CEOS), it marshals federal, state, and local resources to better locate, apprehend, and prosecute individuals who exploit children via the Internet, as well as to identify and rescue victims. For more information about Project Safe Childhood, please visit https://www.justice.gov/psc . Parents are encouraged to always monitor your children’s online activity.

This case was investigated by the Little Rock Police Department with assistance from the Federal Bureau of Investigation and the Arkansas State Police. This case was prosecuted and tried by Assistant United States Attorneys Kristin Bryant and Ashley Bowen.

SEATTLE - The U.S. Marshals (USMS) Pacific Northwest Violent Offender Task Force (PNVOTF) on Oct. 27 arrested a fugitive who was wanted on a felony warrant for attempted rape of a child and communicating with a minor for immoral purposes.
Phillip Wayne Pitts, 50, was wanted by the King County Sheriff’s Office for failing to appear with the original charges of attempted rape of a child and communicating with a minor for immoral purposes.
Pitts was originally arrested on April 5, 2024, during a proactive regional operation led by the Washington Internet Crimes Against Children Task Force ( WA ICAC TF). Hosted by the Seattle Police Department, the WA ICAC TF is a multijurisdictional group of agencies dedicated to the protection of children from sexual abuse and exploitation.
On Feb. 23, after Pitts failed to appear for a court hearing related to the case, the King County Sheriff’s Office issued a felony warrant with a $100,000 bond. The warrant was adopted by the U.S. Marshals Pacific Northwest Violent Offender Task Force.
On Oct. 27, Pitts was located and arrested without incident in the 5400 block of Delridge Way SW in Seattle. He was later booked into the King County Jail.
The PNVOTF is a U.S. Marshals-led partnership composed of federal, state, and local law enforcement officers from Washington, Oregon, and Alaska. The PNVOTF’s primary mission is to locate, apprehend, and return the most violent and egregious federal and state fugitives to the justice system.

Colchester, Vt. – “At midnight it was time to move,” said retired U.S. Army Sgt. 1st Class Pete Ferrell, recalling a night in Afghanistan.
He gripped the handle of one of the four corners of a field stretcher carrying a wounded Soldier. A tray of medical equipment on the Soldier’s chest chirped as it monitored vital signs and sustained him. The team of four Soldiers locked step, carrying the patient onto a plane bound for a higher level of care.
As the plane transporting the wounded Soldier took off, Ferrell found himself on the same runway at Bagram Airfield where the deployment began months earlier. There at the feet of the towering Hindu Kush mountain range, four decades and nearly 3,000 miles stood between him and the jungles he hovered over in a UH-1 “Huey” helicopter in Vietnam, during his first combat tour.
In 2010, at age 62, Ferrell secured an age waiver and volunteered for the deployment to Afghanistan with the Vermont Army National Guard’s 86th Infantry Brigade Combat Team (Mountain).
“He always seeks something bigger than himself to be part of, that’s just who Pete is,” said U.S. Army Maj. Beth Carrier, a physician assistant with the New Hampshire Army National Guard who deployed with Ferrell to Bosnia in 1999 when she was a flight medic. “I can only hope that somewhere in my life that I am a fraction as good of a human as he is.”
For many, it’s hard to imagine that the Vietnam veteran who flew over 250 combat hours as a Huey crew chief and survived being shot down in Laos felt he owed more.
“I never got wounded or had PTSD. I was still capable, and I felt I still had to do more,” said Ferrell.
When he arrived in Da Nang, Vietnam, in 1970 as a helicopter mechanic, he was assigned to the night maintenance shift in a hangar. It was far from the excitement of flying he had imagined as a child in Braintree, Massachusetts, watching planes take off and land at the airport and flying his own model aircraft.
So, he went to his platoon sergeant and asked for a flight platoon assignment. A few days later, the platoon sergeant told him to shadow another Soldier who showed him how to do daily maintenance on a Huey.
“Then he says, ‘OK that one’s yours,’” said Ferrell.
From then on, the 22-year-old specialist was now in charge of his own helicopter.
“We learned a lot about maintenance in training, but overseeing a whole aircraft was a lot of responsibility.”
But along with the added responsibility, he also got his childhood wish.
“When the aircraft flew, you went with it,” he said.
Ferrell said he mostly flew “ash and trash missions” – lift missions that could include transporting anything from troops to supplies to mail.
However, about three months before his tour ended, his unit was selected for Operation Lam 719, a highly contested two-month offensive where they flew South Vietnamese troops into southeastern Laos. The objective was to disrupt North Vietnam’s military supply network on the Ho Chi Minh Trail.
Ferrell said he knew this mission was not routine; the danger felt so imminent that he prayed.
“I started out saying the 23rd Psalm when we took off on the first three sorties, and by the fourth one I must have gotten too comfortable,” he said. “One pilot said to the other, ‘Stay tight to this hill,’ and he no sooner said that and the windshield for the aircraft was blown out.”
The aircraft crashed, but Ferrell and the rest of the crew survived.
“Somebody started yelling, ‘Come on, come on!’” he said, adding that another aircraft had landed nearby and they all started running to it. “I grabbed my M16 and started tromping through the jungle, and we all got on the other aircraft and flew out.”
It wasn’t until Ferrell was on the plane flying home from Vietnam with a ream of military records that he realized he had received 10 Air Medals for his combat flight hours, one with a valor device for the mission on which he was shot down.
He finished his active-duty service in 1973 and settled into civilian life. He married Deb, the woman he exchanged letters with throughout the war, and moved to Vermont where they had their first son.
Then in 1981 he heard a familiar sound and looked up in the Vermont sky and saw Hueys overhead. Ferrell said he knew he had to track them down. He found them in a hangar in Burlington, Vermont, at a Vermont Army Guard aviation unit.
“I walked in and there were 12 Hueys there and it was like a homecoming. I was home again,” he said.
Ferrell met with a flight platoon sergeant who assuaged his fears that if he joined the Guard he might end up sweeping floors rather than maintaining and flying aircraft.
And with that, Ferrell re-enlisted and was back working on Hueys.
In 1998, the unit transitioned to the UH-60 Black Hawk helicopter and assumed a medevac mission. Ferrell was hesitant about learning a new aircraft and mission. That was until he teamed up with Carrier, then a 20-year-old specialist so passionate about her role as a flight medic that she inspired him.
“She taught me that it was all about saving lives, and there’s no better mission than that,” he said.
Ferrell didn’t come around right away, though, Carrier said, adding he refused to do medical training and insisted his job as the crew chief didn’t require it. However, he changed his tune after they medevaced a Soldier with severe appendicitis – their first real-world patient in Bosnia.
After the mission, Ferrell told Carrier that her ability to help the Soldier had captivated him, but he admitted he felt helpless to assist.
“He completely did a 180 on the entire idea of not touching a patient. It was a 100% adjustment of his thought process,” she said. “From then on, he wanted to do all he could, asking ‘What can I do? What can I learn? What can you teach me so I can help you?’”
In turn, he used his knowledge of the aircraft to help her set her medical gear up to deliver care more expediently. These were lessons she would take with her when their careers parted ways, and she deployed to Iraq and later when she was commissioned as an officer and went on to study medicine.
But the two remained close. Ferrell was even the “man of honor” at her wedding, which required him to don a raspberry pink shirt for the occasion.
“I always knew with him I was well protected. On the hoist he could drop me on a dime. I always knew that the aircraft that we were on was the safest that it could possibly be. That was because of Pete's work ethic,” she said.
When Ferrell returned from the Bosnia deployment, personnel moves in the aviation unit led him to move on from aviation. Eventually, he was assigned to the headquarters of the 86th IBCT (MTN), which led to his Afghanistan deployment.
When Ferrell told his wife and sons about volunteering for the deployment, he said they were the only people in his family who didn’t think he was crazy.
“It’s just a part of who he is, and it’s how they [his sons] always knew their father,” said his wife. “So, it was just, he’s going to be gone for a while, but he’ll be back and we will, as we say, improvise, adapt and overcome.”
When he arrived in Afghanistan, his daily duties at the headquarters company kept him mostly at Bagram, but as he had throughout his career, Ferrell felt he still had more to give.
One night he stumbled upon it while sitting in the base’s operations center. A major from another section told him he had a mission at the airfield. Ferrell’s interest was piqued. It turned out that the officer had inadvertently found Ferrell another medevac mission; transferring wounded patients from the field hospital onto aircraft bound to take them to facilities with higher levels of care.
“You know like Beth had taught me, saving lives is the greatest mission there is, and that is what it was,” he said.
He began to stop at the hospital every day after his shift to ask if volunteers were needed that night but never mentioned his side quests to anybody in his unit until years later. He continued the late-night missions until he returned home from Afghanistan just before Christmas 2010.
By then, he was 63 years old, three years past the standard mandatory retirement age, and finally retired from the military in 2011 with 33 years of service.
“You get home from Vietnam, you realize how many men were lost and how many were wounded, and you think, ‘Why me? Why did I survive?’” he said. “You figure out that there is a plan here, so you have to go with it. You take it as the blessing that you were saved for a reason. I can look back now and say that this is where God was pointing me.”
title: From Vietnam to Afghanistan: A Vermont Guard member’s lifetime of service

Lt. Gen. Philip Garrant, Space Systems Command commander, Lt. Gen. Gregory Gagnon, Combat Forces Command commander, and Maj. Gen. James Smith, Space Training and Readiness Command commander, each delivered a keynote address reinforcing the messages of readiness, speed and industry partnership to standing-room-only audiences in town to learn about mission area priorities.
Performing while transforming
“My message is straightforward,” Garrant said. “We are changing how we work: how we connect with operators and mission partners; how we work with industry; and how we equip our workforce to move at the pace the mission demands.”
Garrant listed numerous changes across Space Systems Command in the past year regarding capability, space industry connections and workforce improvements. SSC delivered the final GPS III satellite to orbit in a year that saw a historic launch pace from both coasts. The Victus Haze launch demonstrated that the command could launch within 16 hours from notice to launch and get capability on orbit quickly.
Driving the U.S. Space Force’s Commercial Space Strategy is SSC’s Commercial Space Office (COMSO), which announced that its new Enterprise Space Activity Group (ESAG) and Working Capital Fund executed $1.2 billion across 162 contracts for commercial SATCOM operational capability. COMSO also announced the launch of its new Access to the Classified Ecosystem for Space (ACES), designed to enable better industry participation in war games, exercises and classified events through COMSO-assisted security clearances for companies with a U.S. Department of War sponsor.
Garrant also shared industry feedback demonstrating the command’s progress in hitting small business goals, as well as commercial access, pathways and contract awards, while realistically acknowledging areas where improvements remain underway when it comes to clarity, follow-through and conversion to mission outcomes.
“Next October, we will be right back here at Space Industry Days to show you our work again,” Garrant said. “That is our commitment: continue delivering today’s mission, continue transforming for tomorrow’s fight, and continue being candid about both.”
“What’s going to happen in 15 years?”
In his Oct. 22 keynote, Gagnon began by outlining how the three commands work together.
“In Combat Forces Command, it’s our job to take the people and the kit and turn it into combat-credible, ready-to-fight, ready-to-win forces,” Gagnon explained. “We also have to build the tactics, techniques, procedures and coordinate functions inside the joint force so that spacepower can fuel our ability as a nation, not just to defend ourselves, but to power project.”
Gagnon said there are a lot of things the U.S. Space Force has done right. CFC has operationally accepted more than 50 different capabilities this year, as well as cyber-hardened both weapons systems and installations. He noted that the 16-hour Victus Nox launch, which demonstrated the U.S. Space Force’s ability to rapidly launch and get capability on orbit, “didn’t exist 24 to 36 months ago.”
In 2011, the U.S. Space Force had 18 launches. This year, it is projecting more than 170 — a more than eightfold increase powered by reusable commercial launch. In 2011, one launch equaled about 1.5 satellites in space; today, a single launch can put 50 satellites on orbit.
“Combat realities change quickly,” Gagnon said. “Militaries that adapt, win.”
“We are changing, not just to change,” Gagnon said. “We are changing because we are facing a very aggressive, fast-moving adversary. We are moving fast because we’re in a race and in this race, second place loses.”
CFC has learned several things from major combat operations, Gagnon said. Mobility equals survivability, and it’s not just the ability to “box it up and move,” but the ability to do so repeatedly, Gagnon said. Camouflage, concealment and deception are in vogue again.
“We need to plan and budget for the fact that we will have attrition,” Gagnon said. “Our operations units have just enough equipment to do their job. You need three times the amount of equipment to do your job when you start planning for attrition.”
“What we do, not everyone can do,” Gagnon said. “And I will tell you, our greatest advantage over other militaries is our people. Our people want to be in the military, they volunteered, and they’re highly educated compared to our potential adversaries. U.S. enlisted forces, whether it’s in the maritime services, the space service or the Army, do functions that in foreign militaries are only done by officers. Our people are the special sauce.”
What happens the day after a capability is delivered to the joint force?
Smith explained in his keynote address, “STARCOM’s responsibility begins where a program milestone alone cannot answer the most important question: What happens the day after delivery?”
“Think about everything that’s gone into that moment,” Smith said. “Engineers have solved difficult technical problems, teams have worked requirements and design reviews, and people have made hard choices about costs and schedule. A new capability has reached the force.”
“That is a significant accomplishment, but put yourself in the position of the Guardian who has to use it,” Smith said. “That Guardian needs to understand what the system can do, what its limitations are and how to employ it as part of a larger mission. The force needs tactics to account for those limitations. Commanders need evidence about how the capability will perform under the conditions they expect to face.”
“That’s where the distance between capability, delivery and combat credibility becomes visible,” Smith explained. “STARCOM helps close the distance by developing Guardians, evaluating capabilities and bringing people and systems together with the tactics they need to succeed. Our contribution gives the force a stronger foundation for operational employment.”
“Industry partnership belongs in that work from the beginning,” Smith said. “The choices made during development affect what an instructor can teach, and what a tester can observe. They affect how a capability connects to another system and how quickly supporting training can change. We earn combat credibility by understanding how Guardians, systems and tactics perform together.”
Smith shared how industry can help by designing for trainability so that Guardians can practice the capability they actually operate. Give test teams the data, instrumentation, models and access required to allow Guardians to understand performance under realistic conditions. Industry also can help by designing for integration and adaptation. Interfaces need to be usable across the mission thread, and industry can build technical and business approaches that support meaningful updates at operational speed. Finally, Smith said, industry should stay engaged after the first delivery.
“These are concrete areas where industry can contribute,” Smith said. “Bring us an explanation of the mission problem your approach addresses, and the work it enables. Everyone must be equally clear about the requirements and the evidence we need. That is how industry helps us all forge a combat-credible Space Force.”
title: USSF field command leaders appeal to commercial space industry at Space Industry Days

text:
Congressman Vicente Gonzalez Delivers $800,000 for Safer Streets, Improved Trauma Response to Roadway Crashes
Contact: Alexis Torres
Washington, D.C. – Today, Congressman Vicente Gonzalez (TX-34) announced $800,000 in federal funding for the Rio Grande Valley Regional Advisory Council on Trauma, Service Area V to save lives by reducing the risk of serious injuries on roadways across Cameron, Willacy, Hidalgo and Starr Counties. The funds, allocated through the U.S. Department of Transportation’s (DOT) Safe Streets and Roads for All program, will be used to develop a Comprehensive Safety Action Plan focused on post-crash care and to conduct training at Regional Medical Operations Centers. This work will include regional coordination planning, performance analysis, and piloting real-time trauma resource and prehospital whole blood monitoring technology to improve EMS routing, resource visibility, and survivability.
“Safer streets require stronger investments in our communities. Today’s announcement gives our trauma centers additional resources and support to deliver the best possible care in life-or-death situations where every second matters,” said Congressman Gonzalez. “Since being elected to Congress, I have brought down nearly $8 billion in federal funding to our region, and I will continue working with our federal and local partners to build on these investments to create a better future for South Texas families.
Today’s announcement was made possible by Congressman Gonzalez’s support of the Bipartisan Infrastructure Law, which was enacted in 2021, and authorized $5 billion in appropriated funds over five years (2022-2026) to prevent roadway fatalities and serious injury. The Rio Grande Valley Trauma Regional Advisory Council is committed to improving specialized healthcare to South Texans through education, outreach, collaboration and communication. Trauma Service Area V consists of the four counties, Cameron, Willacy, Hidalgo and Starr, located at the southernmost tip of Texas. There are 13 hospitals in the region and 12 of which serve as trauma-designated facilities.
title: Congressman Vicente Gonzalez Delivers $800,000 for Safer Streets, Improved Trauma Response to Roadway Crashes

William Rondell Lashawn Smith, 44, from Fort Dodge and Des Moines, Iowa, but most recently living in Johnston, Iowa, was sentenced on October 30, 2026, in federal court in Sioux City to 152 months’ imprisonment. Smith pled guilty on April 21, 2026, to one count of conspiracy to distribute methamphetamine, three counts of distribution of methamphetamine and one count of possession with intent to distribute methamphetamine.

Evidence at the plea and sentencing hearings showed that from January 2023 through February 2024, Smith was involved in a conspiracy that distributed more than 14 kilograms of methamphetamine in the Fort Dodge, Iowa area. On three occasions in February 2024, Smith distributed over 2 ½ pounds of methamphetamine to an individual cooperating with law enforcement. On one of those occasions, the distribution occurred within 1,000 feet of Meriwether Park in Fort Dodge. In February 2024, officers searched two of Smith’s properties and seized cocaine, methamphetamine, over $8,000, three firearms, and drug distribution materials, including two scales.

United States District Court Judge Leonard T. Strand sentenced Smith to 152 months’ imprisonment and a ten-year term of supervised release. There is no parole in the federal system. Smith is currently in the custody of U.S. Marshals until he can be transported to a federal prison.

The case was prosecuted by Assistant United States Attorney Shawn S. Wehde and was investigated by Iowa Division of Narcotics Enforcement, Iowa DCI Laboratory, Fort Dodge Police Department, Webster County Sheriff’s Office, Iowa State Patrol, and Bureau of Alcohol, Tobacco, Firearms, and Explosives.

WASHINGTON – Savon Lee Blanchard, 33, a previously convicted killer residing in Temple Hills, Maryland, pleaded guilty today in U.S. District Court in connection with his illegal possession of a Glock 30 pistol that was recovered following a foot chase after police stopped him on a stolen ATV, announced U.S. Attorney Jeanine Ferris Pirro.

Blanchard pleaded guilty before Judge Sparkle L. Sooknanan to one count of unlawful possession of a firearm by a convicted felon. Judge Sooknanan scheduled sentencing for March 2, 2027.

Blanchard was previously convicted in 2016 in Prince Georges County of involuntary manslaughter in the 2011 fatal shooting of 23-year-old Alusine Kargbo of Lanham, who was shot in the back as he played basketball at an elementary school in New Carrollton. For that slaying, Blanchard was sentenced to 10 years in prison with five years suspended for the murder and sentenced to an additional 20 years in prison for use of a handgun in commission of a crime of violence for which he was sentenced to 20 years in prison with 15 years suspended.

According to court documents, on April 17, 2026, about 5:20 p.m., Blanchard was sitting on a white Yamaha Raptor 700R 4-wheeler, an All-Terrain Vehicle (ATV), that was stopped and running near the intersection of Nannie Helen Burroughs Avenue NE and Hayes Street NE. At the same time, Metropolitan Police officers and agents from the Bureau of Alcohol, Tobacco, Firearms and Explosives drove by on patrol.

The stolen Yamaha Raptor ATV.

An MPD investigator attempted to initiate a traffic stop of the ATV and pulled his marked patrol vehicle in front of the ATV to stop it from fleeing. An ATF agent pulled his own patrol vehicle directly behind the ATV.

Blanchard (circled in red) flees from law enforcement. The Glock is circled in yellow.

Blanchard dismounted the ATV and fled on foot. Law enforcement chased Blanchard down the sidewalk. As officers ran, they heard a metal object clank against the sidewalk. One of the agents stopped and recovered a black Glock Model 30 .45 caliber pistol that Blanchard had dropped. The firearm was loaded with 12 rounds in the magazine. Another round was found on the ground near the weapon.

Police recovered this Glock Model 30 and a magazine containing 12 rounds.

Police and ATF agents apprehended Blanchard moments later. A check on the ATV revealed it had been reported stolen out of Anne Arundel County. Subsequently, officers reviewed footage from surveillance cameras that showed them chasing Blanchard, the Glock coming off Blanchard’s person as he ran, and the Glock sliding along the concrete sidewalk.

As a previously convicted felon, Blanchard was prohibited from carrying any firearm.

This case was investigated by the Metropolitan Police Department and the Bureau of Alcohol, Tobacco, Firearms and Explosives, Washington Field Office. The matter is being prosecuted under the Make D.C. Safe and Beautiful initiative by Assistant U.S. Attorney Emory V. Cole. Make D.C. Safe and Beautiful is a law enforcement initiative in support of President Trump’s Executive Order to crack down on gun violence, prioritize federal firearms violations, pursue tougher penalties, and seek detention for federal firearms violators.
